question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
answer:
No. A permanent phasing in does not trigger "when this creature enters" (enters-the-battlefield) abilities, and phasing out doesn't trigger leaves-the-battlefield abilities either.

Phasing is a status, not a zone change: a phased-out permanent is still on the battlefield, but the game treats it as though it doesn't exist and isn't under its controller's control. When it phases in, its status simply changes back to "phased in" and the game treats it as existing again [702.26c], [110.5b]. Because the phasing event doesn't actually move the permanent between zones or change control, zone-change triggers — which include enters-the-battlefield and leaves-the-battlefield triggers [603.6a] — don't trigger when a permanent phases in or out [702.26d]. Effects that check a phased-in permanent's history also won't treat the phasing event as having caused it to enter or leave the battlefield [702.26d].

Similarly, an Aura or Equipment that phases in or out doesn't cause "becomes attached/unattached" triggers to fire [702.26j]. Counters and stickers stay on the permanent throughout [702.26d].

Note that phasing in normally happens as a turn-based action at the start of the active player's untap step, simultaneously with that player's phased-in permanents with phasing phasing out [502.1], [702.26a], [703.4a]. This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games; the only multiplayer wrinkle in the rules provided is that a permanent that phased out under the control of a player who has since left the game phases in during the next untap step after that player's next turn would have begun, and phased-out permanents can leave the game or be exiled when their controller leaves [702.26n], [800.4a].

Zone-change triggers don’t trigger when a permanent phases in or out. Tokens continue to exist on the battlefield while phased out. Counters and stickers remain on a permanent while it’s phased out. Effects that check a phased-in permanent’s history won’t treat the phasing event as having caused the permanent to leave or enter the battlefield or its controller’s control.

answer_gold: No. Phasing in is not a zone change, so it doesn't trigger "enters the battlefield" abilities (or any other zone-change triggers). The permanent was never treated as having left the battlefield in the first place, even though it was ignored while phased out.

question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
answer:
A creature with both trample and deathtouch only has to assign 1 damage to each creature blocking it before the rest can be assigned to the player, planeswalker, or battle it's attacking.

Why: trample says the attacking creature's controller must first assign lethal damage to each blocking creature, and only then may assign excess damage as they choose among the blockers and the attacked player/planeswalker/battle [702.19b]. Deathtouch changes what counts as lethal for that purpose: any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is treated as lethal damage [702.2c], and any damage above 1 from a deathtouch source is excess damage [120.4a].

So a 6/6 with trample and deathtouch blocked by two 4/4s can assign 1 to each blocker and 4 to the defending player. Each blocker still dies, because a creature with toughness greater than 0 that has been dealt damage by a source with deathtouch is destroyed as a state-based action [702.2b], [704.5h]. Note you must still assign at least 1 to each blocker; if you don't assign lethal (here, 1) to every blocker, you can't assign any damage to the player or planeswalker [702.19b]. If all blockers have left combat by the time damage is assigned, all the damage goes to the defending player/planeswalker as though lethal damage had been assigned to them [702.19d].

Terms: 'lethal damage' normally means damage greater than or equal to the creature's toughness, counting damage already marked on it and damage being assigned by other creatures in the same combat damage step [Lethal Damage], [702.19b]. Deathtouch overrides that threshold down to 1 for assignment purposes [702.2c].

One timing note: if the blocker already had damage marked on it, that doesn't matter here — 1 is enough either way with deathtouch. Ordinary trample without deathtouch would let you assign less because of the pre-marked damage [702.19b].

This all works the same in two-player and multiplayer games; the only multiplayer wrinkle is which opponent is the defending player, and the provided rules don't add any special multiplayer assignment rules.

gold_text.702.19b: Trample The controller of an attacking creature with trample first assigns damage to the creature(s) blocking it. Once all those blocking creatures are assigned lethal damage, any excess damage is assigned as its controller chooses among those blocking creatures and the player, planeswalker, or battle the creature is attacking. When checking for assigned lethal damage, take into account damage already marked on the creature and damage from other creatures that’s being assigned during the same combat damage step, but not any abilities or effects that might change the amount of damage that’s actually dealt. The attacking creature’s controller need not assign lethal damage to all those blocking creatures but in that case can’t assign any damage to the player or planeswalker it’s attacking. A 2/2 creature that can block an additional creature blocks two attackers: a 1/1 with no abilities and a 3/3 with trample. The active player could assign 1 damage from the first attacker and 1 damage from the second to the blocking creature, and 2 damage to the defending player from the creature with trample. A 6/6 green creature with trample is blocked by a 2/2 creature with protection from green. The attacking creature’s controller must assign at least 2 damage to the blocker, even though that damage will be prevented by the blocker’s protection ability. The attacking creature’s controller can divide the rest of the damage as they choose between the blocking creature and the defending player.

answer_gold: A trampling creature with deathtouch only needs to assign 1 damage to each blocking creature to count as "lethal damage" to it, then can assign all remaining damage to the defending player/planeswalker. Deathtouch redefines lethal damage: any nonzero amount of combat damage from a deathtouch source counts as lethal for the purpose of trample's damage-assignment rules, so the trampling creature doesn't need to assign damage equal to the blocker's toughness — 1 point per blocker satisfies the requirement.

question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
answer:
Yes. Storm is a triggered ability, and like any triggered ability on the stack it can be countered — but only by an effect that specifically counters abilities, not by a spell that counters only spells.

Details:
- Storm means "When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn. If the spell has any targets, you may choose new targets for any of the copies," and it is expressly a triggered ability that functions on the stack [702.40a].
- When it triggers, its controller puts it on the stack as an object that isn't a card, on top of the spell that has storm; it stays there until it's countered, resolves, or is otherwise removed [603.3].
- Activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren't spells, so "counter target spell" effects can't touch the storm trigger. Effects that specifically counter abilities can counter it [113.9].
- Countering the storm trigger only stops the copies from being created; the original spell with storm is a separate object on the stack and is unaffected. Conversely, countering the original spell doesn't remove the already-triggered storm ability, and the copies it makes will still be created.
- If a spell somehow has multiple instances of storm, each one triggers separately, so each is a separate ability that would have to be countered separately [702.40b].

This works the same way in two-player and multiplayer games; nothing in the storm rules or the ability-countering rule depends on the number of players.

gold_text.113.9: Activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren’t spells, and therefore can’t be countered by anything that counters only spells. Activated and triggered abilities on the stack can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities. Static abilities don’t use the stack and thus can’t be countered at all.

It remains on the stack until it’s countered, it resolves, a rule causes it to be removed from the stack, or an effect moves it elsewhere.

answer_gold: Yes. Storm is a triggered ability that goes on the stack when you cast the spell with storm, and like any triggered ability it can be countered by an effect that specifically counters abilities (e.g. Stifle). It can't be countered by something that only counters spells, because a triggered ability on the stack isn't a spell.

question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
answer:
No. A hybrid mana symbol is all of its component colors, so a card with a symbol like {R/G} has both red and green in its color identity, and you can only include it if *every* color in its color identity is in your commander's color identity ([107.4e], [903.4], [903.5c]).

Color identity is the set of colors of any mana symbols in the card's mana cost or rules text, plus colors from a color indicator or characteristic-defining ability ([903.4]). Reminder text is ignored ([903.4c]), the back face of a double-faced card counts ([903.4d]), and adventurer/alternative characteristics count too ([903.4e]). Rule [903.5c] uses exactly this example: Wort, the Raidmother has color identity red and green, so every card in a Wort deck must be only red, only green, both, or colorless — including every mana symbol in its cost or rules text.

So if your commander is only red, a {R/G} card is illegal in that deck, even though you could always pay the cost with red mana. The card itself is also actually both colors ([202.2d]).

Two exceptions worth knowing:
- Monocolored hybrid symbols like {2/B} are only black (the other half is generic), so such a card is legal with a black commander.
- Colorless-hybrid symbols like {C/W} are only white in color, since the {C} half contributes no color ([107.4e]).

If you have two commanders via partner, use the combined color identity of both ([702.124c]). This all works the same regardless of how many players are at the table.

An object with one or more hybrid mana symbols and/or Phyrexian mana symbols in its mana cost is all of the colors of those mana symbols, in addition to any other colors the object might be. (Most cards with hybrid mana symbols in their mana costs are printed in a two-tone frame. See rule 107.4e.)

question: can I respond to the untap step?
answer:
No. No player receives priority during the untap step, so you can't cast spells, activate abilities, or otherwise "respond" while permanents are untapping [502.4] [117.3a].

Why: the untap step's events are turn-based actions, which happen automatically and don't use the stack [703.1] [703.3]. In order, the untap step is: (1) phasing  ing \u2014 the active player's phased-in permanents with phasing phase out and their phased-out permanents phase in [502.1] [703.4a]; (2) the day/night check, if applicable [731.2]; (3) the active player determines which of their permanents untap and untaps them all simultaneously [502.3] [703.4c]. Because there is no priority, the step simply ends once those actions are complete [500.3].

Anything that triggers during the untap step is held and put onto the stack the next time a player would receive priority, which is normally the upkeep step; those triggers go on the stack before the active player gets priority in the upkeep, and the order they triggered in doesn't matter [502.4] [503.1a] [603.1]. So the earliest you can respond is in the upkeep step, once you have priority [503.1] [117.1].

This is the same in two-player and multiplayer games: the rule is simply that no player receives priority during the untap step, and in the upkeep the active player gets priority first, then it passes in turn order.

question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
answer:
Yes. A creature declared as an attacker (or put onto the battlefield attacking) remains an attacking creature until it's removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first [508.1k] [Attacking Creature] [508.4]. The end of combat step is the fifth and final step of the combat phase [End of Combat Step], so throughout that step the combat phase is still going on and attackers are still attacking.

Removal from combat happens "as soon as the end of combat step ends" — at that point all creatures, battles, and planeswalkers are removed from combat, and then the postcombat main phase begins [511.3] [505.1]. So during the step itself, effects and abilities that check for "attacking creatures" will still see them.

Two related timing points:
- "Until end of combat" effects do NOT expire when the end of combat step begins; they expire at the end of the combat phase [511.2] [500.5a]. Abilities that trigger "at end of combat" trigger as the step begins, and the active player gets priority [511.1] [511.2].
- A creature can even be put onto the battlefield attacking during the end of combat step; it enters as an unblocked attacking creature [508.4d].
- Individual creatures can stop being attacking creatures earlier if something removes them from combat — leaving the battlefield, changing controller, phasing out, regenerating, ceasing to be a creature, or an effect that specifically removes them [506.4] [506.4a]. Also, an effect that ends the combat phase (e.g., Mandate of Peace) removes everything from combat immediately rather than waiting [724.2d].

This is the same in two-player and multiplayer games; nothing here depends on the number of players, though in multiplayer each attacking creature is attacking a particular defending player, a planeswalker they control, or a battle they protect [508.4].

So any "as long as this creature is attacking" effect or ability that cares about attacking status is still live for the whole end of combat step.

question: Do you cast lands?
answer:
No. You never cast a land — you *play* it. Playing a land is a special action: the player simply puts the land card onto the battlefield from the zone it's in (usually their hand), and it doesn't use the stack [305.1] [116.2a] [701.18a].

Key consequences:
- Because the land never goes on the stack, it's never a spell, it can't be countered, and players can't respond to it with instants or activated abilities [305.1] [505.6b].
- You may do this only when you have priority, during a main phase of your turn, with an empty stack, and only once per turn unless an effect lets you play additional lands [116.2a] [505.6b] [701.18a]. You can't play a land at all on someone else's turn [305.3].
- Lands are put onto the battlefield without paying any cost; most lands have no mana cost at all [202.1b].
- If a card is both a land and another type (e.g. an artifact land), it can only be played as a land, never cast as a spell [300.2a] [305.9].
- "Play a card" on an effect means play it as a land or cast it as a spell, whichever is appropriate — casting only applies to the nonland case [601.1a] [701.18b]. Older cards that said "play" a spell have been errata'd to "cast" [601.1].
- An effect that *puts* a land onto the battlefield is not playing a land and doesn't use up your land play for the turn [305.4].

By contrast, a creature card (or other nonland spell) from your hand is cast, and that does use the stack [302.1].

This is the same in two-player and multiplayer games; the land-play restriction is tied to your own turn and your own priority [305.3] [116.2a].

question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
answer:
Yes. Evoke's sacrifice is a triggered ability, not part of the cost, so it uses the stack and players get priority before it resolves — you can sacrifice the evoked creature to some other cost or ability (for example, an exploit trigger or a sacrifice cost) during that window.

How it works: "Evoke [cost]" means "You may cast this card by paying [cost] rather than paying its mana cost" and "When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it" [702.74a]. That second, triggered part goes on the stack the next time a player would receive priority [603.3d], and it only resolves once all players pass in succession [608.1]. That gap is your chance to act.

If you sacrifice the creature yourself in the meantime, the evoke trigger still resolves but can do nothing, because the permanent it would sacrifice is no longer on the battlefield; an ability exists on the stack independently of its source and uses last known information as needed [113.7a]. Your own sacrifice is a real sacrifice, so abilities that trigger "when a player sacrifices a permanent" (and leaves-the-battlefield abilities) still see it — those triggers look back in time [603.10a]. Likewise, if the evoke trigger is the one that resolves first, that sacrifice is a sacrifice too, and you no longer have the creature available for another cost.

Timing caveat: this assumes you sacrifice it after the evoke trigger is already on the stack. You could also sacrifice it in response to something before the trigger is put on the stack only if a player would get priority earlier, which normally doesn't happen — the trigger is put on the stack at the first such opportunity [603.3d].

This reasoning doesn't depend on player count; it's the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
answer:
Yes. Keyword abilities are just abilities written in shorthand, so an effect that removes all abilities removes them too. Rule 702.1 explains that a keyword is simply the name of an ability that's very common or too long to spell out, with reminder text summarizing it — flying, trample, lifelink and the rest are abilities in every rules sense.

Supporting details:

- Rule 113.10 and 113.10b: an effect that removes an ability says the object "loses" it, and effects that remove an ability remove all instances of it. "Loses all abilities" therefore sweeps up keyword abilities, triggered abilities, activated abilities, and static abilities alike.
- Rule 613.1f: ability-removing effects apply in layer 6, alongside ability-adding effects and keyword counters. Timestamp/dependency order in that layer decides the outcome if abilities are both added and removed; in general the most recent effect prevails (rule 113.10c). So a keyword granted after the "loses all abilities" effect's timestamp can still stick.
- Rule 113.12: things that aren't abilities are not removed. An effect setting a characteristic ("[permanent] is red") or stating a quality ("[creature] can't be blocked") isn't an ability, so losing all abilities doesn't undo those. Likewise, a characteristic-defining ability's text is an ability and is removed, but note rule 604.3 for how CDAs otherwise function.
- Rule 603.6b: if the loss of abilities applies the moment a permanent is on the battlefield, its enters-the-battlefield triggered ability never triggers.

This is a general rules answer and doesn't change between two-player and multiplayer games.

answer_gold: Yes. Keyword abilities (like flying, trample, deathtouch) are abilities — the keyword is just shorthand printed on the card for a full chunk of rules text or a defined ability. An effect that strips "all abilities" removes keyword abilities along with any other activated, triggered, or static abilities the object has.

question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
answer:
Yes. Maximum hand size (normally seven) is not a cap on how many cards you can hold at any moment; it only matters once, during your cleanup step. Rule 402.2 says a player may have any number of cards in their hand, but as part of their cleanup step must discard down to the maximum hand size. So if you already have seven cards and an effect tells you to draw, you draw normally and simply hold eight (or more).

The only consequence is timing-based: immediately after the cleanup step of your own turn begins, if your hand has more cards than your maximum hand size, you discard enough to get down to it as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [514.1] [703.4n]. If you drew the extra cards on someone else's turn, you keep them through that turn — the discard only happens in the active player's cleanup step.

Two caveats unrelated to hand size: cards are drawn one at a time [121.2b], and if you're required to draw more cards than remain in your library, you draw what's left and lose the game the next time a player would receive priority [104.3c]. Also note maximum hand size can be modified by other effects — for example, a Vanguard card with a -1 hand modifier makes your maximum hand size six, so you'd discard down to six at cleanup [902.5b].

This works the same whether you're playing with two players or more than two; the discard always happens in the active player's cleanup step, so in a multiplayer game each player trims their own hand only during their own turn's cleanup step.

question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
answer:
A planeswalker with 0 loyalty is put into its owner's graveyard immediately, as a state-based action [704.5i], [306.9]. Loyalty is a characteristic only planeswalkers have, and a planeswalker's loyalty on the battlefield equals the number of loyalty counters on it [306.5], [306.5c]. So "0 loyalty" means "no loyalty counters on it."

Details:
- State-based actions don't use the stack; they're checked and performed automatically whenever a player would receive priority, so no one can respond to the planeswalker dying [704.1].
- Loyalty can reach 0 by damage (damage dealt to a planeswalker removes that many loyalty counters from it) [120.3c], [306.8], or by activating a negative loyalty ability, where [-N] means "remove N loyalty counters" [107.7].
- You can't actually go below 0: a planeswalker never has fewer than zero counters, since counters simply stop being removed once none remain; the planeswalker is put into the graveyard at 0 [122.1e]. Excess damage beyond the remaining loyalty is simply excess.
- The card goes to its owner's graveyard, not the controller's [704.5i].

This works identically in two-player and multiplayer games — the rule is about the planeswalker's own loyalty and doesn't depend on the number of players.

question: do non-creature artifacts die?
answer:
Short answer: no — "dies" is reserved for creatures. A noncreature artifact that's destroyed or sacrificed is simply "put into its owner's graveyard from the battlefield"; it doesn't die, and abilities that trigger on something dying won't see it. (If an artifact is also a creature — an artifact creature — then it does die when it's put into a graveyard from the battlefield.)

Grounding available in the provided context: [603.10a] gives the example of an artifact with "Whenever a creature dies, you gain 1 life" that is destroyed alongside two creatures by a mass destruction spell. The ability triggers exactly twice — once for each creature — even though the artifact itself went to the graveyard at the same moment. The artifact's own trip to the graveyard is not counted as a death, which shows the term tracks creatures only. Note also that leaves-the-battlefield/dies-style triggers "look back in time" per [603.10a], so simultaneous destruction doesn't stop the creature triggers.

Caveat on completeness: the rule that formally defines "dies" (the glossary/rule 700.4-style definition) was not included in the context I was given, so the above is inferred from the [603.10a] example rather than quoted from the definition itself. Separately, a noncreature artifact going to the graveyard is still a leaves-the-battlefield event, so abilities worded "When [this] is put into a graveyard from the battlefield" or "leaves the battlefield" do trigger for it ([603.6c]).

Nothing here differs between a two-player game and a multiplayer game; and regardless of player count, an object going to a graveyard always goes to its owner's graveyard ([400.3]).

However, some triggered abilities are exceptions to this rule; the game “looks back in time” to determine if those abilities trigger, using the existence of those abilities and the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event. The list of exceptions is as follows: Some zone-change triggers look back in time. These are leaves-the-battlefield abilities, abilities that trigger when a player sacrifices a permanent, abilities that trigger when a card leaves a graveyard, and abilities that trigger when an object that all players can see is put into a hand or library. Two creatures are on the battlefield along with an artifact that has the ability “Whenever a creature dies, you gain 1 life.” Someone casts a spell that destroys all artifacts, creatures, and enchantments. The artifact’s ability triggers twice, even though the artifact goes to its owner’s graveyard at the same time as the creatures.

The ability could be unable to find the object because the object never entered the specified zone, because it left the zone before the ability resolved, or because it is in a zone that is hidden from a player, such as a library or an opponent’s hand. (This rule applies even if the object leaves the zone and returns again before the ability resolves.) The most common zone-change triggers are enters-the-battlefield triggers and leaves-the-battlefield triggers. Leaves-the-battlefield abilities trigger when a permanent moves from the battlefield to another zone, or when a phased-in permanent leaves the game because its owner leaves the game. These are written as, but aren’t limited to, “When [this object] leaves the battlefield, . . .” or “Whenever [something] is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, . . . .” (See also rule 603.10.) An ability that attempts to do something to the card that left the battlefield checks for it only in the first zone that it went to. An ability that triggers when a card is put into a certain zone “from anywhere” is never treated as a leaves-the-battlefield ability, even if an object is put into that zone from the battlefield.

answer_gold: Yes. The rules define "dies" generically for any permanent, not just creatures. Rule 700.4 is the entire definition: “The term dies means ‘is put into a graveyard from the battlefield.’” That wording isn't restricted to creatures, so a non-creature artifact that goes from the battlefield to a graveyard (destroyed, sacrificed, or otherwise) technically “dies” under the rules, just like a creature would. Players often use “dies” conversationally as if it only applied to creatures, but per the actual rules text it applies to any permanent, artifacts included.

question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
answer:
You lose the game — but not instantly. Attempting to draw from an empty library doesn't do anything immediately; instead, the next time a player would receive priority, a state-based action is checked and you lose the game [121.4] [704.5b] [104.3c].

Details:

- "Draw" means putting the top card of your library into your hand, either as the turn-based action in your draw step or as part of a cost or effect [121.1] [504.1]. With no cards in the library, no card moves, but the attempt is recorded.
- State-based actions don't use the stack and are checked automatically before any player gets priority [704.1]. So if you'd draw multiple cards from a nearly-empty library, you draw the remaining ones and then lose [104.3c]. You can still finish resolving the current spell or ability first.
- Having an empty library does not make drawing "impossible." If an effect offers you the choice to draw, you may choose to do so even with an empty library [121.3] [608.2d] — and if an effect replaces the draw (for example, replacing it with something else), that replacement still applies even though there were no cards to draw, so you don't lose [121.6a] [614.11].
- Contrast with milling and with effects that move cards from library to hand without the word "draw": those aren't draws, so an empty library doesn't kill you that way. You can't mill more cards than are in your library; if instructed to, you mill as many as possible [701.17b] [609.3] [121.5].

Multiplayer: the rules given here are worded per player, not per two-player game — the player who attempted the empty draw loses the game, and the rest of the table plays on. In a two-player game that same loss ends the match.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming you actually attempted the draw. If instead your library merely became empty and nothing has asked you to draw yet, nothing happens — an empty library by itself is not a loss condition; you'd lose only on the next attempted draw (typically your next draw step).

question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
answer:
The combat phase has five steps, in this order: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat [506.1]. Two of those can be skipped or doubled: if no creatures are declared as attackers or put onto the battlefield attacking, the declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped [506.1][508.8]; and there are two combat damage steps if any attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike [506.1].

As the defending player, you never get priority first in a step. Priority is the system that determines who may cast spells, activate abilities, or take special actions [117.1]. In each combat step the step's turn-based actions happen first (they don't use the stack), then the active player receives priority, and you get priority only after the active player passes. The context spells this out explicitly for the end of combat step: it has no turn-based actions, and once it begins the active player gets priority [511.1].

Step by step:
- Beginning of combat: turn-based action first if it's a multiplayer game where not all of the active player's opponents automatically become defending players 	heir opponents to be the defending player [507.1][703.4h]. Then the active player gets priority, then you. This is your last window to act before attackers are declared.
- Declare attackers: attackers are declared as a turn-based action, then players get priority.
- Declare blockers: you declare blockers as a turn-based action immediately after the step begins, and that declaration does not use the stack [509.1][703.4j]  ldeclaring blocking. You get priority only after blockers are already declared and the active player passes.
- Combat damage: immediately after the step begins, each player announces damage assignment in APNAP order \u2014 the active player announces how each attacking creature assigns damage, then the defending player announces how each blocking creature assigns damage [510.1][703.4k]. All that damage is then dealt simultaneously, and no player can cast spells or activate abilities between assignment and dealing [510.2]. Priority comes only after damage has been dealt.
- End of combat: no turn-based actions; active player gets priority, then you [511.1].

Two players vs. multiplayer: in a two-player game the nonactive player is automatically the defending player [506.2a]. In multiplayer, there may be one or more defending players depending on the variant and options (e.g., the attack multiple players option [802.1], attack left/right [803.1]); unless all of the active player's opponents automatically become defending players, the active player chooses one opponent as a turn-based action during the beginning of combat step, and that player becomes the defending player [506.2a][507.1]. Under the shared team turns option, combat damage is announced by the active team then the defending team [805.10f].

Note also that some spells are restricted to "only before/after" a particular point in combat, such as "attackers are declared" or "the combat damage step" [506.7], so check such cards against these step boundaries.

question: can i respond to a mana ability?
answer:
No. Mana abilities don't use the stack, so they can't be targeted, countered, or responded to — they resolve immediately upon being activated (or, for triggered mana abilities, immediately after the mana ability that triggered them) [113.4] [605.3b] [605.4a] [405.6c].

A "mana ability" is an activated or triggered ability that could produce mana and doesn't use the stack [Mana Ability] [605.1]. Practical consequences:

- There's no window between activation and resolution in which anyone can act. If you had priority before the mana ability was activated, you get priority again after it resolves, and only then can you cast a spell or activate a (non-mana) ability [405.6c].
- Players can activate mana abilities without priority: whenever they have priority, whenever they're casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment, or whenever a rule or effect asks for a mana payment — even mid-cast or mid-resolution [117.1d] [605.3a] [608.2g].
- You can still respond to the *spell or ability* the mana was used for, once it's on the stack and players get priority — just not to the mana ability itself.
- Watch for lookalikes: an ability with a target is not a mana ability, and a spell is never a mana ability, so those do use the stack and can be responded to normally [605.5a] [605.5b].

question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
answer:
No. Paying a cost is not something you can respond to — costs are paid as part of a single, uninterrupted action (casting a spell, activating an ability, or declaring attackers/blockers), and no player gets priority in the middle of it.

How it works when casting a spell: the whole sequence of proposing the spell, determining and locking in the total cost, activating mana abilities, and paying is one action performed by the caster [601.2a] [601.2f] [601.2g] [601.2h]. The only "window" that exists is for the caster themself to activate mana abilities before payment, and mana abilities don't use the stack [118.2] [601.2g] [605.1]. Other players can't act until the spell is fully cast and someone next receives priority. The same is true for costs paid during declaring attackers [508.1i] [508.1j] and declaring blockers [509.1e] [509.1f] — those turn-based actions don't use the stack, and costs are paid in full with no partial payments.

Practical consequences:
- Because the total cost is locked in before payment, effects that would change it afterward do nothing [601.2f]; likewise, activating a cost-altering ability won't affect anything already on the stack [602.4].
- You can only respond after the fact — e.g., after the spell is on the stack and fully paid for, when you next get priority. At that point you can respond to the spell, but the payment has already happened and can't be undone.
- If the player turns out to be unable to complete payment, the action is illegal and is reversed rather than "responded to" [733.1] [118.3].

Assumption on timing: I'm reading "respond" as casting a spell or activating a non-mana ability in the middle of someone paying. If you instead meant responding to a triggered ability that triggered off the payment, that ability goes on the stack and you may respond to it normally once a player receives priority.

This applies the same regardless of the number of players; the provided rules on declaring attackers and blockers and on priority don't change with more than two players, though in multiplayer the specific opponent whose costs you'd want to interact with may differ.

question: can you explain layers?
answer:
Layers are the game's ordering system for applying continuous effects to determine an object's current characteristics. You start with the actual object — for a card, its printed characteristics; for a token or a copy of a spell/card, the characteristics defined by the effect that created it — and then apply every applicable continuous effect in a fixed sequence of layers [613.1]. The game does this continually and automatically, and all resulting changes are instantaneous [613.5].

The layers named in the provided rules are:
- Layer 1: rules and effects that modify copiable values [613.1a]. Layer 1 has sublayers, starting with layer 1a, copy effects and merge-with-permanent changes; "as . . . enters"/"as . . . is turned face up" abilities generate copiable effects if they set power and toughness [613.2a]. After all of layer 1 is applied, the object's characteristics are its copiable values [613.2c], which is what a copy effect picks up [707.2].
- Layers 2–6 include control-changing (layer 2), type-changing (layer 4), color-changing (layer 5), and layer 6, ability-adding effects, keyword counters, ability-removing effects, and effects saying an object can't have an ability [613.1f], [613.6].
- Layer 7 (power/toughness) is broken into sublayers [613.4]; layer 7b sets power and/or toughness to a specific number or value, and layer 7c applies effects and counters that modify power/toughness without setting them [613.4c], [613.5].

Ordering within a layer: in layers 2–6, characteristic-defining abilities apply first, then all other effects in timestamp order [613.3], [604.3]; within each layer 1 sublayer and each layer 7 sublayer, effects apply in timestamp order [613.2], [613.4]. An earlier timestamp applies before a later one [613.7]. Dependency can override timestamp order: an effect depends on another if they're in the same layer/sublayer, applying the other would change the first effect's text, existence, what it applies to, or what it does, and neither (or both) come from characteristic-defining abilities [613.8], [613.8a]. Effects can also simply override one another, in which case the later timestamp "wins" [613.9].

One effect can split across layers: "gets +1/+1 and becomes the color of your choice" applies its color part in layer 5 and its +1/+1 part in layer 7c, and once it starts applying to a set of objects it keeps applying to them in each later layer even if its source is removed [613.6].

Worked example from the rules: Gray Ogre is a 2/2. A +1/+1 counter (layer 7c) makes it 3/3; "+4/+4 until end of turn" (7c) makes it 7/7; "Creatures you control get +0/+2" (7c) makes it 7/9; then "becomes 0/1 until end of turn" applies in layer 7b — earlier than all of those — so the result is 0/1 plus +4/+4, +0/+2, and +1/+1, i.e. 5/8 [613.5], [613.4c].

Effects that affect players rather than objects (like giving a player protection from red) aren't in the layer system; they're applied in timestamp order after objects' characteristics are determined [613.10].

None of this depends on player count, so it works identically in two-player and multiplayer games. Note also that the provided context doesn't spell out layers 3 (text-changing) or 7a/7d, so I've only described the layers actually given.

question: how does the legend rule work?
answer:
The legend rule is a state-based action: if a single player controls two or more legendary permanents with the same name, that player chooses one of them to keep, and all the rest are put into their owners' graveyards [704.5j] [Legend Rule].

Key points:

- It's keyed on name, not on card type. Two different legendary creatures with different names are fine; two copies of the same-named legendary permanent under one player's control are not [704.5j].
- It's per player. Two different players may each control a legendary permanent with the same name at the same time with no problem — the rule only triggers on permanents "controlled by the same player." This is true whether the game has two players or more than two [704.5j].
- It applies to any permanent with the legendary supertype [205.4d], including tokens created as legendary tokens [111.9] and planeswalkers, which now carry the legendary supertype instead of the removed "planeswalker uniqueness rule" [306.4] [Planeswalker Uniqueness Rule (Obsolete)].
- Being a state-based action, it happens automatically as soon as the condition exists, doesn't use the stack, and can't be responded to [704.1]. The permanents put into the graveyard go to their owners' graveyards, not the controller's [704.5j].
- Cards that are legendary only on their flipped side aren't legendary until flipped, so the legend rule doesn't apply beforehand [710.2].
- Don't confuse it with the "world rule," which is timestamp-based and keeps the newest world permanent rather than letting you choose [704.5k].

Note that legendary instants and sorceries aren't permanents; they instead have a casting restriction requiring you to control a legendary creature or legendary planeswalker [205.4e].

question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
answer:
Your creature is destroyed the moment the game next checks state-based actions — which happens immediately, before any player would receive priority — not at some later step and not as part of the damage event itself.

Details:

- "Lethal damage" means total damage marked on the creature greater than or equal to its toughness [Lethal Damage], [120.6].
- Damage itself doesn't destroy anything; neither the damage nor its source kills the creature. Destruction happens as a state-based action based on the resulting game state [120.5], [302.7], [704.5g].
- State-based actions don't use the stack and can't be responded to [704.1]. They're checked and performed every time a player would get priority, repeatedly until nothing more happens, and only then does a player get priority [704.3], [117.5], [117.2d].
- Because state-based actions ignore what happens mid-resolution, a creature that momentarily has lethal damage marked (or toughness 0) during the resolution of a spell or ability won't die if the condition is gone once resolution finishes [704.4].
- Regeneration can replace this destruction, and regenerating removes all damage marked on the creature [704.5g], [120.6].
- Related: a source with deathtouch destroys the creature via a separate state-based action regardless of the amount [702.2b], [704.5h]; and a creature with toughness 0 or less is put into its owner's graveyard instead, which regeneration can't replace [704.5f].
- If somehow the creature is not destroyed (e.g., toughness was raised above the marked damage), the marked damage stays until the cleanup step, when all marked damage is removed [120.6], [514.2].

This timing is the same regardless of the number of players; state-based action checks aren't player-count dependent.

Regeneration can replace this event.

All damage marked on a creature is removed when it regenerates (see rule 701.19, “Regenerate”) and during the cleanup step (see rule 514.2).

question: can I cast my commander from exile?
answer:
No — not just because it's your commander. Rule 903.8 only lets you cast a commander you own from the command zone; it grants no permission to cast it from exile. Under rule 601.3f, you can begin to cast a spell only if some rule or effect allows it, so a commander sitting in exile can't be cast unless a separate effect (for example, an effect that specifically lets you cast that card from exile) grants that permission.

What usually happens instead: if your commander is put into exile (or a graveyard), rules 903.9a and 704.6d give a state-based action letting its owner put it into the command zone, provided the object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked. Once it's in the command zone, you may cast it under rule 903.8, paying an additional {2} for each previous time you've cast it from the command zone that game (commander tax) — that extra cost is generic mana, on top of the card's normal mana cost, whose colored symbols are unchanged. Note that if you decline the state-based action at that check, the commander stays in exile and this window doesn't come back.

Also relevant: rule 903.3d confirms the commander designation is an attribute of the card that persists in every zone, including exile — but that designation alone is not permission to cast it from exile.

This all works the same regardless of how many players are at the table; Commander is typically multiplayer, and none of the rules above depend on the player count.

If a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone. This is a state-based action. See rule 704.

question: what happens during the cleanup step?
answer:
During the cleanup step — the second and final step of the ending phase — three things happen, in order:

1. Discard to hand size: if the active player's hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard enough cards to get down to that number. This is a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [514.1] [703.4n].

2. Damage removal and end-of-turn effects: immediately after that discard, simultaneously all damage marked on permanents (including phased-out permanents) is removed and all "until end of turn" and "this turn" effects end. Also a turn-based action, not using the stack [514.2] [703.4p].

3. Normally no player gets priority, so no spells can be cast and no abilities activated [514.3] [117.1]. The exception: the game checks for state-based actions and for triggered abilities waiting to go on the stack (including abilities that trigger "at the beginning of the next cleanup step"). If any exist, the state-based actions are performed, the triggered abilities are put on the stack, and then the active player gets priority and players may cast spells and activate abilities. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins, and the process repeats [514.3a] [704.3] [608.1].

If nothing needed doing on that first check, no player gets priority and the step simply ends as soon as its actions are complete [704.3] [500.3]. As the step ends, effects lasting until end of that step expire and any unspent mana in players' mana pools empties [500.5] [703.4q].

question: when are state-based actions checked?
answer:
State-based actions are checked every time a player would receive priority — and they're handled before that player actually gets it.

How the check works: when a player would get priority, the game first looks for any of the listed state-based action conditions and performs all applicable ones simultaneously as a single event [704.3], [117.5]. If any were performed, the check repeats; if none were performed, any triggered abilities waiting to be put on the stack are put on the stack, and then the check repeats again. Only once a check performs no state-based actions and no triggered abilities are waiting does the appropriate player actually receive priority [704.3], [117.5], [117.2d].

Key points:
- State-based actions happen automatically, are not controlled by any player, and don't use the stack [704.1], [704.2], [405.6f]. An ability that watches for a game state and triggers is a triggered ability, not a state-based action [704.1a], [603.1].
- Turn-based actions come first: when a step or phase begins, its turn-based actions are dealt with before state-based actions are checked, before triggered abilities go on the stack, and before anyone gets priority [703.3], [117.3a], [703.1].
- Cleanup step: the same check process occurs, but if the step's first check performs no state-based actions and no triggered abilities are waiting, no player gets priority and the step ends [704.3], [514.3a]. If something is found, the state-based actions are performed, triggered abilities go on the stack, and the active player does get priority [514.3a]. (Discarding to maximum hand size in cleanup is a turn-based action, not a state-based action [514.1].)
- Combat damage step: state-based actions are performed, and abilities that triggered on damage or during those state-based actions go on the stack, before the active player gets priority [510.3a].
- Effects that end the turn or end the combat phase also check state-based actions, but afterward no player gets priority and no triggered abilities are put on the stack [724.1c], [724.2c].

This timing is the same regardless of how many players are at the table; the rules provided are not player-count dependent, though in a multiplayer game "the appropriate player" who would get priority is determined by normal turn order [117.1], [117.3a].

question: when can I concede a game?
answer:
You can concede at any time — literally any point in the game, regardless of whose turn it is, whether you have priority, or whether spells or abilities are on the stack. Conceding means quitting the game: you leave the game immediately and lose it [104.3a] [Concede].

Details worth knowing:

- Conceding doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to; it happens immediately [405.6g].
- It's the one thing that no card can override. Normally a card's text beats a general rule, but rule [101.1] specifically carves out conceding as the sole exception — no card can stop you from conceding.
- If another player is controlling you (a "mind control" style effect), that player still cannot make you concede, and you may still concede yourself at any time even while controlled [723.6] [723.5b].
- Multiplayer note: the rules given here apply to any number of players — a concession removes just that one player from the game. One provided variant rule matters: in Two-Headed Giant, if a player concedes, their whole team leaves the game and loses immediately [810.8b].
- Tournament note: tournaments have additional rules layered on top of the game rules [100.6], and a judge can also cause a player to lose a game via penalty [104.3k], but nothing in the provided rules restricts when you may concede.

The provided context doesn't cover concession-related sportsmanship or bribery restrictions from the tournament documents, so treat the above as the game-rules answer.

question: how do I know who the active player is?
answer:
The active player is simply the player whose turn it is; every other player is a nonactive player [102.1]. So you identify the active player by looking at whose turn is currently being taken — there's no other test needed.

A few clarifications that follow from that:

- Combat: during the combat phase the active player is the attacking player. In a two-player game the nonactive player is the defending player [506.2]. In a multiplayer game where the active player's opponents don't all automatically become defending players, the active player chooses one opponent to be the defending player as a turn-based action at the beginning of the declare attackers step [507.1].
- Priority: the active player receives priority at the start of most steps and phases (e.g., [504.2], [505.6], [507.2], [508.2], [509.2], [510.3]), and priority determines who may cast spells or activate abilities [117.1].
- Simultaneous choices: when several players must choose at once, the active player chooses first, then each nonactive player in turn order (usually clockwise), and the actions happen simultaneously — the APNAP rule [101.4], [101.4e]. While starting the game, the starting player counts as the active player [101.4e].
- Mind control effects: if a player is being controlled by another player during their own turn, they are still the active player; only control of the player changes [723.3].
- Team/shared-turn games: with the shared team turns option, teams take turns, so there's an active team and nonactive teams [805.4a], and choices go active-team-first, players on a team in any order they like [805.6]. An ability referring to "the active player" in such a game refers to one specific active player, chosen by the ability's controller when the effect is applied [805.9].

question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
answer:
The player who cast the spell gets priority first — even if that player is not the active player. Rule 117.3c: if a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority again afterward. So a nonactive player who casts a spell keeps priority and may cast another spell or activate abilities before passing.

Once that nonactive player passes, priority moves to the next player in turn order, and the spell on the stack resolves only when all players pass in succession (608.1). After the spell resolves, priority goes to the active player, not back to the spell's controller (117.3b).

This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games; the only difference is that in multiplayer, after the caster passes, priority travels through each remaining player in turn order before the spell resolves. Note that priority isn't the same as the order in which players make choices while a spell is resolving or being cast — that uses APNAP order, active player first (101.4, 101.4d), with the exception in 601.7b for spells that instruct an opponent to make a choice during casting.

question: when the active player cast a spell, who gets priority first?
answer:
The active player who cast the spell keeps priority — they receive it again immediately after the spell is cast, before any opponent gets a chance to respond.

Priority is the system that determines which player may cast spells, activate abilities, or take special actions at a given moment [117.1]. Rule 117.3c states that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward. Rule 601.2i says the same thing at the end of the casting process: once the spell becomes cast (and any "when you cast" triggers are put on the stack), if the spell's controller had priority before casting it, they get priority again.

So the sequence is: active player has priority → casts the spell → active player again has priority (they could cast another instant, activate an ability, or pass). Only when the active player passes does priority move to the next player in turn order. In a two-player game that's the single opponent; in a multiplayer game it passes to each other player in turn order, one at a time, and the spell resolves only after all players pass in succession.

If you instead meant who gets priority after the spell *resolves*: that's also the active player, per rule 117.3b. And any opponent who casts something while your spell is still on the stack has cast it "in response," so theirs resolves first [117.7].

question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
answer:
Yes. Whenever you cast a spell while you have priority, you receive priority again immediately afterward, so you can cast another spell (or activate an ability) before anyone else gets a chance to respond [117.3c] [601.2i] [116.3]. This is what players call "holding priority": you simply don't pass, and you keep casting. You can repeat this as many times as you like, stacking multiple spells on top of each other; they'll resolve in reverse order (last cast, first to resolve) [117.7].

A few points to keep in mind:

- You must be in a step or phase where players get priority, and each spell must be legal to cast at that time (e.g. sorceries only when the stack is empty during your main phase) [601.3]. In the cleanup step no player normally gets priority at all, though there's an exception when state-based actions or triggers occur, after which the active player gets priority and spells can be cast [514.3] [514.3a].
- After each of your spells resolves, the active player gets priority again — not automatically you [117.3b]. So holding priority matters for stacking spells before any of them resolve.
- The step or phase won't end while you keep adding to the stack; it ends only when the stack is empty and all players pass in succession [500.2].
- You cannot hold priority in the middle of a spell's resolution: if a resolving spell or ability lets you cast a spell, no player receives priority after that spell is cast, so you can't chain extra spells that way [608.2g]. Likewise, no player gets priority during the process of an effect ending the combat phase [724.2f].

This works identically with two players and with more than two players — you keep priority after each cast, and only when you pass does priority move on to the other players in turn order.

question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
answer:
Lore counters are put on Sagas at the start of each player's own precombat main phase — as a turn-based action immediately after that main phase begins, the active player puts one lore counter on each Saga they control that has one or more chapter abilities. This doesn't use the stack, so no player can respond before the counter is placed (though the resulting chapter ability triggers do use the stack) [703.4f] [505.4] [714.3c].

Details:

- Only in the precombat main phase, not the postcombat main phase, and only for Sagas controlled by the active player. In a multiplayer game this means each player triggers their own Sagas on their own turn; the rules provided contain no different multiplayer behavior. In an Archenemy game, it happens after the archenemy's scheme action [703.4f].
- Immediately after the lore-counter placement, if the active player controls Attractions, they roll to visit them [703.4g].
- Sagas also get counters on entry, not from this turn-based action: a Saga without read ahead enters with one lore counter on it [714.3a], and a Saga with read ahead enters with a chosen number of lore counters between one and its final chapter number [714.3b] [702.155b]. These are replacement effects [614.1c].
- A chapter symbol "{rN}—[Effect]" means "When one or more lore counters are put onto this Saga, if the number of lore counters on it was less than N and became at least N, [effect]" — so placing the counter is what triggers chapter abilities [714.2b] [107.15a]. Read ahead restricts this: chapter abilities can't trigger the turn the Saga entered unless it has exactly the number of counters named in that chapter symbol [702.155a].
- Once the number of lore counters is greater than or equal to the Saga's final chapter number and it isn't the source of a chapter ability still on the stack, its controller sacrifices it as a state-based action [714.4] [704.5s].

question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
answer:
A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by an effect that instructs a player to do something later in the game rather than right when the effect is created. [Delayed Triggered Ability] [610.2]

Key points from the rules:

- Wording: it contains "when," "whenever," or "at," though that word usually isn't the first word of the ability (e.g. "Exile this creature at the beginning of the next end step"). [603.7] [603.7c] Compare a normal triggered ability, written "[When/Whenever/At] [trigger event], [effect]" [603.1].
- How it's created: during the resolution of a spell or ability, as the result of a replacement effect being applied, or as a result of a static ability that lets a player take an action. [603.7a] A permanent spell with a static ability that functions on the stack creates its delayed triggered ability as the permanent enters the battlefield. [608.3g]
- It won't trigger until it has actually been created, even if the trigger event just happened; and earlier events can make the trigger event impossible (a "when this creature leaves the battlefield" delayed ability never triggers if the creature already left before the creating spell resolved). [603.7a]
- Duration: it triggers only once, the next time its trigger event occurs, unless it states a duration like "this turn." If the event happens more than once simultaneously with no stated duration, its controller picks which occurrence triggers it. [603.7b]
- Objects it tracks: it still affects a referenced object even if that object changes characteristics, but not if the object has left the expected zone (or left and returned, making it a new object). [603.7c] [400.7]
- Source and controller: if a spell created it, the spell is the source and the spell's controller as it resolved is the controller [603.7d]; if an activated or triggered ability created it, that ability's source and controller apply [603.7e]; for replacement effects or static-ability actions, the object with the static ability is the source [603.7f] [603.7g]. This is one of the exceptions to the usual controller rules. [109.4b] [108.4]
- Stack use: effects themselves don't use the stack, but delayed triggered abilities do go on the stack when they trigger. [405.6a]
- Special cases: an ability may create a delayed triggered ability that triggers when the creating ability has resolved a certain number of times in a turn; that delayed ability is created only once [603.7h]. If it refers to X without defining it, X equals the X chosen for the spell or ability that created it. [107.3n]

Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
answer:
Yes. Instant and sorcery spells — the non-permanent spells — do have abilities.

Most of an instant's or sorcery's text is a spell ability: an ability followed as instructions while that instant or sorcery spell is resolving. Any text on an instant or sorcery is a spell ability unless it's an activated ability, a triggered ability, or a static ability meeting the criteria of rule 113.6 [113.3a] [Spell Ability].

So non-permanent spells can also carry the other categories of abilities:

- Static abilities, which are simply true statements that do something all the time rather than being activated or triggered [604.1]. Some static abilities apply while a spell is on the stack — often ones referring to countering the spell, plus "As an additional cost to cast…," "You may pay [cost] rather than pay this spell's mana cost," and "You may cast this without paying its mana cost" [604.5]. Others apply while the card is in a zone you could cast it from (usually your hand), limited to "You may cast this card…," "You can't cast this card…," and "Cast this card only…" [604.6].
- Triggered abilities, which trigger whenever the game event matches their trigger event, regardless of zone restrictions that apply and even when it isn't legal to cast spells [603.2a].

In general, abilities of an instant or sorcery spell usually function only while that object is on the stack (as opposed to abilities of other objects, which usually function only on the battlefield), with exceptions such as those in 604.6 [113.6]. Note also that an activated or triggered ability on the stack is its own object and is not a spell, so it can't be countered by something that counters only spells [113.1c] [113.9].

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; it applies the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
answer:
Yes. Split second is a static ability that says "As long as this spell is on the stack, players can't cast other spells or activate abilities that aren't mana abilities" [702.61a]. Mana abilities are explicitly excluded from that restriction, so any player may still activate mana abilities (and take special actions) while a spell with split second is on the stack [702.61b].

A mana ability is an activated or triggered ability that produces mana and meets the criteria in rule 605.1; activated mana abilities don't use the stack and resolve immediately, so they can't be responded to [605.1] [605.3b] [113.4]. You may activate one whenever you have priority, or whenever you're paying a cost that requires mana [605.3a] [117.1d]. If you had priority before activating it, you get priority back afterward [405.6c].

Note what this does not let you do: you can't activate a non-mana ability in response, and triggered abilities (including triggered mana abilities' non-mana counterparts) still trigger and go on the stack normally [702.61b]. So mana floating from a mana ability is only useful for things you're still allowed to do \u2014 which, with split second on the stack, generally means nothing but more mana abilities and special actions.

This works the same regardless of the number of players: split second restricts all players equally, and each player may still activate their own mana abilities [702.61a].

Triggered abilities trigger and are put on the stack as normal while a spell with split second is on the stack." So mana abilities (and special actions) are untouched by split second; only non-mana activated abilities and casting other spells are locked out.

question: How many zones does the game normally use, and which of them belong to one player rather than being shared by everyone?
answer:
There are normally seven zones: library, hand, battlefield, graveyard, stack, exile, and command. Some older cards also use an eighth, the ante zone [400.1].

Of these, three are per-player: each player has their own library, hand, and graveyard. The others \and command \ battlefield, stack, exile, and command (plus ante where it applies) \ are shared by all players [400.1]. Note this is true regardless of the number of players; in a multiplayer game each player still has a personal library, hand, and graveyard, while the battlefield, stack, exile, and command zone remain common to the whole table [400.1].

A related but separate distinction is public vs. hidden: graveyard, battlefield, stack, exile, ante, and command are public zones (all players can expect to see the faces), while library and hand are hidden zones, even if every card in one happens to be revealed [400.2]. Also, "outside the game" is not a zone \ an object is outside the game if it isn't in any of the game's zones [400.11], and a "junkyard" pile of cards put into the command zone is likewise not its own zone [717.6a].

Some older cards also use the ante zone. Each player has their own library, hand, and graveyard. The other zones are shared by all players.

Library and hand are hidden zones, even if all the cards in one such zone happen to be revealed.

question: Is a player's library a hidden zone or a public one, and can a player look through or rearrange the order of their own library whenever they like?
answer:
A library is a hidden zone, and no — you may not look at your library or change its order whenever you like.

Hidden zones are zones in which not all players can be expected to see the cards' faces; the library and hand are the hidden zones, and they stay hidden zones even if every card in one of them happens to be revealed. The public zones are graveyard, battlefield, stack, exile, ante, and command [400.2].

Each library must be kept as a single face-down pile, and players can't look at or change the order of cards in a library [401.2]. More generally, the order of objects in a library can't be changed except when an effect or rule allows it [400.5]. So you only get to see or reorder library cards when something specifically tells you to — for example, an effect that lets you look at or reveal the top card [401.5], a scry [701.22c], a search [701.23f], a shuffle [701.24b], or an effect that puts two or more cards into a specific position in a library at once, in which case their owner may arrange them in any order and doesn't reveal that order [401.4].

What any player may always do is count the number of cards remaining in any player's library, at any time [401.3]. Contrast this with your hand, which you may arrange however you like and look at any time, though other players may only count it [402.3].

This is the same at any table size: the rules on library privacy don't change between two players and multiplayer. In multiplayer, if several players would look at or reorder library cards simultaneously (e.g. multiple players scrying), the choices are made in APNAP order — active player first, then the rest in turn order — and the cards move simultaneously [101.4], [701.22c].

Library and hand are hidden zones, even if all the cards in one such zone happen to be revealed.

question: Are cards a player has exiled public information by default, or can a player keep them secret?
answer:
By default, exiled cards are public information. Exile is a public zone, meaning all players can see the faces of cards there except for those that a rule or effect specifically allows to be face down [400.2]. Exiled cards are kept face up by default and may be examined by any player at any time [406.3].

A player can keep exiled cards secret only when a spell or ability specifically exiles them "face down." Such cards can't be examined by any player except when an instruction allows it [406.3]. If a player was instructed to look at a card and then exile it face down, or is otherwise once allowed to look at a face-down exiled card, that player may keep looking at it for as long as it remains in exile (until it leaves exile or is shuffled into a pile), even after the permission-granting instruction no longer applies [406.3]. A card exiled face down has no characteristics, and if the effect lets it be played, it's turned face up just before the player announces they're playing it (unless it's being cast face down) [406.3a]. Notably, a player may only begin to cast a spell from among face-down exiled cards if they are allowed to look at that card [601.3f], [406.3b].

Practical bookkeeping rules limit how much secrecy helps: face-down exiled cards must be kept in separate piles based on when and how they were exiled, and if a player must choose an exiled card without being allowed to look at it, they choose a pile and a card is picked at random from it (not revealed until the cost is fully paid, if choosing is part of casting or activating) [406.4], [601.2i]. Exiled cards that might return or that matter due to their abilities should also be kept in separate, trackable piles [406.5]. Foretold cards specifically must be differentiable from each other and from other face-down exiled cards the player owns, including their exile order and any altered foretell costs [702.143e]. A double-faced card exiled face down stays hidden using a substitute card and/or opaque sleeves [712.17], [713.1].

One clarification: a face-down card in exile has nothing to do with the "face down" status of a permanent on the battlefield — only permanents have status [110.5d].

This is the same in two-player and multiplayer games; the rules on exile's publicness make no distinction by player count. In multiplayer, "any player" simply means every player at the table may examine face-up exiled cards.

question: When a permanent is destroyed and moves from the battlefield to the graveyard, is it still the same game object it was on the battlefield, or does something change about its identity?
answer:
It becomes a brand-new object. When a permanent is destroyed and moves from the battlefield to its owner's graveyard, the card in the graveyard is a new object with no memory of, or relation to, its previous existence as a permanent on the battlefield (rule 400.7; see also 403.4, which says the reverse when something enters the battlefield). So counters, damage marked on it, Auras/effects that were affecting it, and anything it "remembered" are gone — the graveyard card doesn't carry them.

There are limited exceptions where the game can still connect the two:

- Abilities that trigger on an object changing zones can find the new object it became in the zone it moved to, provided that zone is a public zone (the graveyard is public) — rules 400.7e and 603.6e/603.6c. Note that such an ability checks only the first zone the card went to, and if the card has since left that zone (even if it returned) the ability won't find it (603.6, 603.6c).
- Abilities that trigger when an enchanted permanent leaves the battlefield can find the new objects that the Auras on it became in their owner's graveyard, including Auras put there by the state-based action for being unattached (400.7f, 704.5m).
- If an effect (or a spell/ability's cost) moves an object to a public zone, later parts of that same effect can find it there (400.7j).
- Leaves-the-battlefield abilities "look back in time," using how objects appeared immediately before the event to decide whether they trigger (603.10, 603.10a).
- Delayed triggered abilities referring to a specific object won't affect it if it's no longer in the expected zone, and a card that left and returned is a new object (603.7c).

Two other identity notes: exiling an already-exiled object isn't a zone change, but it still becomes a new object that has just been exiled (400.8, 406.7); and merging keeps the same object rather than creating a new one (730.2c).

None of this depends on player count — the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: If an effect would put an instant or sorcery card onto the battlefield, what actually happens to it?
answer:
Nothing happens to it — the instant or sorcery card simply stays where it already was. If an effect would put an instant card onto the battlefield, it remains in its previous zone instead [304.4], and the same is true for a sorcery card [307.4]. This is the general principle that cards of certain card types can't enter certain zones [400.4a].

So, for example, an effect that says "return target card from your graveyard to the battlefield" applied to a sorcery card leaves that card sitting in the graveyard; it is not exiled, not put into the graveyard from somewhere else, and it doesn't briefly touch the battlefield.

A related case: a double-faced spell that would enter the battlefield with an instant or sorcery face up doesn't enter the battlefield at all and is instead put into its owner's graveyard [712.13a]. Likewise, if an effect instructs a player to transform or convert a permanent into an instant or sorcery face, nothing happens [712.10]. And if a player is told to put a modal double-faced card onto the battlefield and its front face isn't a permanent card, the card stays in its current zone [712.14b].

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; it applies identically in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: If a token is moved off the battlefield (to a hand, graveyard, exile, or anywhere else), what happens to it, and can it ever come back?
answer:
It ceases to exist, and it can never come back.

When a token leaves the battlefield, it does actually go to the new zone (graveyard, exile, hand, library, etc.) momentarily, so leave-the-battlefield and zone-change triggered abilities do trigger [111.7]. But a token in any zone other than the battlefield ceases to exist as a state-based action — checked automatically the next time state-based actions are performed, without using the stack [111.7, 704.5d, 704.1].

Once it has left the battlefield, it's stuck: a token that has left the battlefield can't move to another zone or return to the battlefield. If some effect would move it (for example, a graveyard-recursion or flashback-style effect, or "return that card to the battlefield"), it simply remains in its current zone and then ceases to exist at the next state-based action check [111.8]. So an effect that exiles a token "and returns it at end of turn" will never bring it back.

One related distinction: phasing out is not a zone change. A phased-out token is still on the battlefield and continues to exist normally, so phasing doesn't destroy tokens [702.26d].

Also note that a token isn't a card, so effects that only affect cards in other zones don't apply to it anyway [111.6].

This answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games; the only multiplayer-specific wrinkle in the provided rules is that a token that would be created under the control of, or owned by, a player who has left the game is simply not created [800.4b, 800.4d].

question: Can players freely rearrange the order of objects on the stack, the way they might rearrange permanents on the battlefield?
answer:
No. The order of objects on the stack is fixed and can't be freely rearranged; it can change only when an effect or rule specifically allows it [400.5]. The stack tracks the order in which spells and abilities were added, and each new object goes on top of everything already there [405.2]; a spell being cast becomes the topmost object as it's put on the stack [601.2a], as does a triggered ability when it's put on the stack [603.3b]. Objects resolve one at a time from the top down as players pass priority [608.1], so the recorded order matters and players can't shuffle it around.

By contrast, objects on the battlefield (and in other non-ordered, non-face-down-pile zones) may be arranged however their owners wish, as long as control, tapped/flipped status, and attachments stay clear to all players [400.5]. Libraries, graveyards, and face-down piles are ordered like the stack and likewise can't be reordered at will [400.5].

The legitimate 'choose an order' moments are narrow and rule-granted, not free rearrangement:
- When an effect puts two or more objects on the stack at the same time, the active player's objects go on lowest, then each other player's in APNAP (Active Player, Nonactive Player) order; a player controlling several of them picks their relative order [405.3, 101.4].
- When multiple abilities have triggered since a player last got priority, each player in APNAP order chooses the order of their own triggers as they're put on the stack [603.3b].
- Similar owner's-choice ordering exists for cards entering a graveyard simultaneously [404.3], cards put into a library at once [401.4], and components of a merged permanent leaving the battlefield [730.3a].

Multiplayer note: the APNAP ordering rules above are written for any number of players, so with three or more players each nonactive player, in turn order, sets the order of their own objects/triggers after the active player [405.3, 101.4, 603.3b]. Two special formats change the structure rather than allowing free rearranging: in Two-Headed Giant (team) play, the active team orders all of its triggers, then each nonactive team in turn order [805.7]; and Grand Melee games have multiple stacks, with rules dictating which stack a spell or ability must go on [807.5b].

The same is true for objects arranged in face-down piles in other zones. Other objects in other zones can be arranged however their owners wish, although who controls those objects, whether they’re tapped or flipped, and what other objects are attached to them must remain clear to all players.
