question: Does every turn always include all five phases (beginning, precombat main, combat, postcombat main, ending), even if nothing happens during some of them?
answer:
Yes — by default every turn contains all five phases in order: beginning, precombat main, combat, postcombat main, and ending, and each phase takes place even if nothing happens during it [500.1]. The beginning, combat, and ending phases are further divided into steps that proceed in order [500.1], [501.1], [506.1], and no game events can occur between steps, phases, or turns [500.12].

Two qualifications:

1. Effects can skip phases. To skip a phase is to proceed past it as though it didn't exist; "skip [something]" is a replacement effect meaning "instead of doing [something], do nothing" [500.11], [614.10], [614.10b]. Once a phase has started it can no longer be skipped — the skip waits for the next occurrence [614.10b]. So a card that skips your combat phase, for example, does remove that phase from that turn.

2. Steps within a phase can be skipped or doubled even when the phase itself happens. The declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped if no creatures are declared as attackers or put onto the battlefield attacking, and there are two combat damage steps if any attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike [506.1]. Also, some steps never give priority — no player receives priority during the untap step, and normally none during the cleanup step [117.3a], [500.3], [514.3] — but the step still happens; its turn-based actions are performed automatically without using the stack [703.1], [703.3].

So "nothing happening" never removes a phase; only a skip effect does. This is true regardless of the number of players — nothing in the phase-structure rules depends on the player count.

Each of these phases takes place every turn, even if nothing happens during the phase. The beginning, combat, and ending phases are further broken down into steps, which proceed in order.

question: In a two-player game, does the player who takes the very first turn get a draw step on that turn?
answer:
No — in a two-player game the player who takes the very first turn skips their draw step entirely on that turn [103.8a]. It isn't just that they don't draw a card; the whole step is skipped, so nothing happens during it (no turn-based draw action, no priority during that step) [504.1, 703.4d]. That player's first turn therefore goes untap step, upkeep step, then straight to the main phase, even though the beginning phase normally consists of untap, upkeep, and draw [501.1].

Note that this only applies to the first turn of the player who plays first; every later turn has a normal draw step, in which the active player draws a card as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [504.1, 703.4d].

For tables with more than two players: in multiplayer games other than Two-Headed Giant, the starting player does not skip the draw step of their first turn [103.8c, 800.7]. In a Two-Headed Giant game, the team that plays first does skip the draw step of its first turn [103.8b, 810.6], and in formats where teams take turns, each player on the team draws during that team's draw step [805.4b].

answer:
No. In a free-for-all multiplayer game with three or more players, the starting player does NOT skip the draw step of their first turn — they draw as normal [800.7], [103.8c].

So on the starting player's first turn in a free-for-all, the draw step happens normally and the active player draws a card as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [504.1]. Every other player in turn order also draws on their own turns as usual.

question: In a Two-Headed Giant game, does the team that takes the first turn skip its draw step, and if a step isn't skipped, does each player on a team normally draw their own card during that team's draw step?
answer:
Yes to both. In a Two-Headed Giant game, the team that plays first skips the draw step of its first turn [103.8b] [810.6] [800.7]. And in any draw step that isn't skipped, each player on the active team draws their own card during that team's draw step [805.4b].

Details:
- Two-Headed Giant uses the shared team turns option, so teams take turns rather than individual players [810.2] [805.4b]. The skip applies to the whole team's first turn, not just one player [805.8].
- Because more than one player is drawing at once, the draws aren't literally simultaneous: each player on the active team performs their draws in whatever order that team likes, then each player on each nonactive team in turn order does the same [121.2d] [805.6a]. Cards are always drawn one at a time [121.2d].
- Contrast with other formats: in a two-player game the player who plays first skips their first draw step [103.8a], while in multiplayer games that aren't Two-Headed Giant, no player skips the first draw step [103.8c] [800.7].
- This also holds for larger "Three-Headed Giant" style variants using the same rules; each player on the team still draws in that team's draw step [810.11] [805.4b].
- Note the team-loss risk: if a player tries to draw from an empty library, that player loses and so does the whole team [810.8a].

question: If a player is given several extra turns at once by different effects, in what order are those extra turns actually taken?
answer:
They're taken in reverse order of creation: the most recently created extra turn is taken first. Extra turns are added directly after the specified turn, and if a player is given multiple extra turns, they're added one at a time; the last one added sits closest to the current turn, so it happens first (rule 500.7). This is the same last-in, first-out pattern used for extra phases and steps (rules 500.8 and 500.9).

If several extra turns are created simultaneously (for example, by one event that causes multiple abilities to trigger), the order of creation is determined by the order the abilities resolve, and the last one to resolve/create its turn is the one taken first.

Multiplayer note: if extra turns are given to more than one player at the same time, they're added one at a time in APNAP order 	urorder order 	starting with the active player (rules 500.7 and 101.4), and again the most recently added turn is taken first. In a two-player game APNAP is simply active player then the opponent. Two variants change this: with shared team turns, the player's whole team takes the extra turn (rule 805.8), and in Grand Melee the extra turn may be delayed depending on turn markers \u2014 if a turn marker is within three seats to the player's left the extra turn waits, and if one is within three seats to their right the player passes the marker and takes the extra turn immediately before their next turn (rule 807.4i), and a player with no turn marker at that time takes the extra turn just before their next turn instead (rule 807.4j).

question: If an effect would cause a player to skip their next upkeep, but their upkeep has already started by the time that effect resolves, does the upkeep get retroactively skipped?
answer:
No. Once a step has started, it can no longer be skipped; the skip effect simply waits and applies to the next upkeep step that occurs [614.10], [614.10a]. "Skip [something]" is a replacement effect meaning "instead of doing [something], do nothing" [614.10b], [614.1b], [Skip], and a replacement effect can only replace an event that is still about to happen — it can't undo something already in progress [614.1]. To skip a step is to proceed past it as though it didn't exist [500.11], which is impossible for a step already underway.

So if the effect resolves during the upkeep step (which is possible, since the active player gets priority once the upkeep step begins and spells/abilities can be cast and resolve then [503.1], [117.1], [608.1]), that upkeep continues normally to its end, and the very next upkeep step that would occur is the one skipped instead. Note also that anything already scheduled for a skipped step won't happen, and anything waiting for the "next" occurrence waits for the first non-skipped one [614.10a]; if two such skip effects are in place, the player must skip the next two upkeeps [614.10a].

Timing assumption: I'm reading the question as the effect finishing resolution after the upkeep step has already begun. If instead the effect resolved earlier in the turn (e.g., during the untap step's held triggers or a prior phase) or on a previous turn, then the upkeep step in question would never begin at all and would be skipped outright. Since no player receives priority during the untap step, effects can't resolve there — triggers wait until upkeep [502.4].

This analysis doesn't depend on player count: the rules cited apply the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: If several triggered abilities controlled by different players all trigger from the same event, in what order are they put on the stack?
answer:
They go on the stack in APNAP order: the active player puts all such triggered abilities they control on the stack first (choosing the relative order among their own), then each nonactive player in turn order does the same [603.3b] [101.4]. Because the stack resolves top-down (last on, first off), the active player's abilities are placed lowest and therefore resolve last, while the last nonactive player's abilities resolve first [405.3].

Details worth knowing:

- Nothing happens at the moment an ability triggers; each triggered ability waits and is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority [117.2a] [117.5]. Its controller is the player who controlled its source when it triggered [109.4b].
- The order in which the abilities actually triggered is irrelevant — only APNAP order and each player's own choice matter. The combat and step rules restate this explicitly for abilities triggering on attackers being declared [508.2b], blockers being declared [509.2a], damage being dealt [510.3a], and at the beginning of upkeep [503.1a].
- There is a two-part process within APNAP: first, in APNAP order, each player puts on the stack the triggered abilities they control whose trigger condition is not "another ability triggering"; second, in APNAP order, each player puts on the remaining triggered abilities (those that trigger off abilities triggering) [603.3b].
- After that, the game checks state-based actions again and puts any newly triggered abilities on the stack, repeating until nothing new happens; then the appropriate player gets priority [603.3b] [117.5].

Two players vs. more than two: the rule is the same procedure either way. With exactly two players it collapses to "active player's abilities go on the stack first, then the nonactive player's." With three or more, the nonactive players follow in turn order (normally starting with the player to the active player's left) [101.4]. Note the provided context also includes variant-format rules: in a Two-Headed Giant-style team game the active team places all abilities its members control first, then each nonactive team in turn order [805.7], and Grand Melee games use multiple stacks, so a player must specify which stack a triggered ability goes on [807.5b].

question: Because the active player's simultaneously-triggered abilities are placed on the stack before a nonactive player's, does that mean the active player's version of the trigger actually resolves first or last relative to the nonactive player's?
answer:
Last. Because the active player puts their simultaneously-triggered abilities on the stack first, those abilities end up lowest on the stack, and the stack resolves top-down — so the nonactive player's trigger (placed on top later) resolves first, and the active player's resolves afterward.

Why: when multiple abilities have triggered since the last time a player received priority, they're put on the stack in APNAP order — active player first, then each nonactive player in turn order (rules 603.3b, 101.4). Rule 405.3 states the same idea explicitly for simultaneous placement: objects controlled by the active player are put on lowest, followed by each other player's objects in APNAP order. A player controlling several such abilities chooses their relative order. Resolution then proceeds one object at a time from the top of the stack each time all players pass in succession (rule 608.1), which reverses the placement order — hence "active player places first, resolves last." This is the same principle behind casting spells "in response": the later-added object resolves first (rule 117.7).

With more than two players it works identically, just extended: active player's triggers go on lowest, then the next player in turn order, and so on, so the last nonactive player in turn order has their triggers on top and resolving first, with the active player's resolving last. Note the order in which the abilities actually triggered doesn't matter (e.g., rules 508.2b, 509.2a, 510.3a, 503.1a); only APNAP placement does. Also, within 603.3b's two-part process, abilities that triggered off another ability triggering are placed in a second pass, so they go on top of the first batch and resolve before it.

(For Two-Headed Giant games, rule 805.7 substitutes teams for players: the active team places all of its triggers first, so they likewise resolve last.)

question: Do static abilities ever get put on the stack the way triggered and activated abilities do?
answer:
No. Static abilities never use the stack. They are written as statements that are simply true, doing something all the time rather than being activated or triggered [604.1] [113.3d], and the continuous effects they generate don't go on the stack [405.6b] [117.2b]. Priority doesn't apply to them [117.2b].

A practical consequence: because they never go on the stack, static abilities can't be countered at all — effects that counter spells or that counter activated/triggered abilities have nothing to target [113.9]. You also can't respond to a static ability the way you can respond to a triggered or activated ability going on the stack.

When do they apply? A static ability's continuous effect is active as long as the permanent with the ability is on the battlefield and has the ability, or as long as the object with the ability is in the appropriate zone [604.2] [611.3b]. The effect isn't 'locked in' — it applies at any moment to whatever its text indicates [611.3a]. Some static abilities function in other zones: characteristic-defining abilities function in all zones, outside the game, and before the game begins [604.3], and some static abilities function while a spell is on the stack, such as ones about countering the spell, additional casting costs, or 'you may cast this without paying its mana cost' [604.5]. Even in those cases the static ability itself is not an object on the stack — it's just applying to the spell that is.

A related edge case: a static ability that functions on the stack can create a delayed triggered ability (as with dash, blitz, or warp), and that delayed trigger is created as the permanent enters the battlefield [608.3g]. Likewise, a static ability can create a one-shot effect giving a spell an ability as it's put on the stack [610.5] [601.2a]. Those resulting triggered abilities do use the stack, but the static ability that made them does not.

This is true regardless of the number of players; nothing here depends on a two-player game.

question: If a targeted spell or ability is about to resolve and every single one of its targets has become illegal, what happens to it?
answer:
It doesn't resolve at all. On resolution the game checks each target's legality; if every target, for every instance of the word "target," is illegal, the spell or ability is removed from the stack and none of its effects happen. If it's a spell, it's put into its owner's graveyard; if it's an ability, it simply ceases to exist [608.2b]. Note this is not the same as being countered by a spell, but the practical result is the same: nothing it would have done occurs, including parts that don't involve the target (e.g., Sorin's Thirst's controller gains no life if the targeted creature is illegal) [608.2b].

A target is illegal if it no longer exists, is no longer in the zone it was in when targeted, or no longer meets the spell's or ability's requirements (changed characteristics, gained protection, etc.) [Illegal Target] [608.2b].

If even one target is still legal, the spell or ability resolves normally, and the illegal targets just aren't affected by the parts of the effect for which they're illegal [608.2b].

Permanent spells work similarly: an Aura spell whose only target is illegal doesn't resolve and goes to its owner's graveyard [608.3b] [608.3c]. Two exceptions: a bestowed Aura spell with an illegal target stops being an Aura and resolves as a creature spell entering the battlefield [702.103e] [608.3b], and a mutating creature spell with an illegal target resolves as an ordinary creature spell entering the battlefield [702.140b].

Also relevant: spells and abilities can affect objects they don't target, and those aren't chosen until resolution [115.10] — but if all actual targets are illegal, the spell or ability never resolves, so those untargeted effects never happen either. Nothing here depends on the number of players; the rule works identically in two-player and multiplayer games.

The steps described in rule 608.2n and 608.2p are followed last. If the spell or ability specifies targets, it checks whether the targets are still legal. question: If a spell has two targets and only one of them becomes illegal before it resolves, does the whole spell fail, or does it still resolve and just skip the illegal target?
answer:
It still resolves. A spell only fails to resolve if *all* of its targets — for every instance of the word "target" — are illegal when it tries to resolve. With two targets and one still legal, the spell resolves, but the illegal target isn't affected by any part of the effect for which it's illegal [608.2b].

Details:
- "Illegal target" means a target that no longer exists (it left the zone it was in when targeted) or no longer meets the spell's targeting requirements — e.g. it gained protection, changed characteristics, or the spell's text changed [608.2b] [Illegal Target].
- On resolution, targets are checked first [608.2b]. If at least one is legal, the spell resolves normally; parts of the effect aimed at the illegal target simply don't happen, and any continuous rules-affecting effects it would create don't apply to that target [608.2b] [613.11].
- If part of the effect needs information about the illegal target, it fails to get that information and anything depending on it doesn't happen [608.2b]. The Plague Spores example in [608.2b] shows a permanent that is illegal for the "target nonblack creature" part but still legal for the "target land" part — it still gets destroyed by the land part.
- Caveat for single-target-with-rider spells: the Sorin's Thirst example in [608.2b] shows that if the spell's only target is illegal, nothing at all happens — not even the "you gain 2 life" rider.
- Special cases: an "exchange" effect is all-or-nothing — if the whole exchange can't be completed, no part of it occurs, so a two-target exchange spell does nothing to the surviving target [701.12a]. And for a permanent spell with an illegal target, it doesn't resolve at all unless it's a bestowed Aura or mutating creature spell, which instead resolve as ordinary creature spells [608.3b].

This rule works identically in two-player and multiplayer games; targeting legality is checked per target, and a target player who has left the game is treated as no longer being there [115.9b].

question: If an effect lets a player "choose new targets" for a spell or ability, must every one of the original targets actually be replaced?
answer:
No. When an effect lets a player "choose new targets" for a spell or ability, the player may leave any number of the original targets unchanged — including all of them — even if those unchanged targets would now be illegal. If the player does change some or all of the targets, each new target must be legal, and the change must not cause any unchanged target to become illegal [115.7d].

A few related points:
- Only the final set of targets is checked for legality, so targets can be swapped around among themselves [115.7e].
- If the spell or ability divides or distributes an effect (like damage or counters) among its targets, the original division can't be changed [115.7f].
- Choosing new targets never lets you change a modal spell's or ability's mode [115.8].
- Contrast "change the target(s)," where each target can only be changed to another legal target and, if they can't all be changed, none of them are [115.7a]; "change a target" (exactly one may be changed) [115.7b]; and "change any targets" (any number may be changed) [115.7c].
- The same permissive rule applies when an effect copies a spell or ability and says its controller may choose new targets for the copy [707.10c].

This is independent of player count — it works the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: If an effect lets a player "change the target(s)" of a spell (as opposed to "choose new targets"), can they change a target to something that isn't a legal target for that spell?
answer:
No. Under "change the target(s)," each target can only be changed to another legal target for that spell.

Details:

- "Change the target(s)" is all-or-nothing: every target must be changed to a different legal target, and if not all of them can be, none of them are changed. If a particular target can't be changed to another legal target, that original target stays put — even if it has since become an illegal target itself [115.7a].
- Related variants work the same way except for how many targets change: "change a target" lets exactly one target be changed [115.7b], and "change any targets" lets any number be changed [115.7c]; in both, any changed target must still be a legal target.
- The contrast with "choose new targets": there, the player may leave any number of targets unchanged even if those targets are now illegal, but any target the player does change must be changed to a legal one, and the new choices must not make an unchanged target illegal [115.7d]. So under neither wording can you point a spell at something that isn't a legal target — the only difference is whether already-illegal targets may be left alone.
- Only the final set of targets is checked for legality, so targets can be swapped among each other [115.7e]. Also, the same object or player can't be chosen twice for one instance of "target" [115.3], an existing division of damage or counters can't be rearranged [115.7f], and you can't change the mode of a modal spell this way [115.8, 700.2f].
- If a target is illegal when the spell tries to resolve, that part of the effect simply doesn't apply to it, and if all targets are illegal the spell doesn't resolve at all [608.2b].

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; it applies the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Can a spell or ability on the stack ever legally target itself?
answer:
No. A spell or ability on the stack is always an illegal target for itself [115.5]. This holds even for spells that can target other spells or abilities on the stack: rule [115.2] permits targeting objects like spells and abilities that can't exist on the battlefield, but [115.5] carves out the object itself as an illegal choice.

A couple of related points so this stands on its own:

- Targets are chosen as the spell is cast or as the ability is put on the stack [115.1], [115.1a], [115.1d], [603.3d], and can't be changed afterward except by an effect that explicitly says so [115.7].
- If a spell or ability uses the word "target" more than once, the same object may be chosen once per instance of "target" [115.3]  be be one of those choices, again because of [115.5].
- A copy of a spell or ability is a new object on the stack; when new targets are chosen for a copy [707.10c], the copy still can't target itself, though a copy and its original are different objects, so one could target the other if the wording allows targeting a spell or ability.

This answer is independent of player count \player game or a multiplayer table \u2014 nothing in the targeting rules provided makes this differ, though note that in a Grand Melee game with multiple stacks a spell or ability must be put on the same stack as its target [807.5b].

question: If a spell or ability requires targets but its wording lets the caster choose any number of them, is choosing zero targets a legal choice, and if zero are chosen, is that spell or ability still considered "targeted"?
answer:
Yes — if the spell or ability's wording allows "any number of" targets, choosing zero is a legal choice, and if zero targets are chosen the spell or ability is not treated as targeted.

Details:

- A spell or ability that requires targets may allow zero targets to be chosen. It is still described as a spell or ability that "requires targets," but it is targeted only if one or more targets were actually chosen for it [115.6]. So with zero chosen, nothing that checks "targets [something]" or "a spell that targets" will find a target, and effects that care about being targeted (including "can't be the target of spells" style protection) simply never come into play for it.

- The choice is made while casting/putting the ability on the stack: for a spell with a variable number of targets, the caster announces how many targets they will choose before announcing them, and once that number is determined it doesn't change even if the information used to determine it changes [601.2c]. Declaring "zero" locks that in — you can't add targets later.

- Note the distinction between targeting and merely affecting: a spell or ability can still affect objects and players it doesn't target, and those are generally not chosen until resolution [115.10, 115.10a]. So choosing zero targets doesn't necessarily mean the spell does nothing; only the target-dependent portion does nothing.

- Related but separate: modal spells and cost-dependent effects (kicker, bargain, teamwork) only require their targets if that mode or cost was chosen; otherwise the spell is cast as though it did not have those targets [700.2c, 702.33g, 702.166d, 702.194c].

This is the same in two-player and multiplayer games; none of the provided rules make the number-of-targets choice depend on the number of players.

question: What single word most commonly marks an effect as a replacement effect rather than some other kind of continuous effect?
answer:
"Instead." Effects that use the word "instead" are replacement effects; most replacement effects use "instead" to indicate what event is being replaced with another event [614.1a] [Instead].

A replacement effect is a continuous effect that watches for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replaces it with a different event, acting like a "shield" around whatever it affects [614.1].

Other wordings also mark replacement effects even without "instead": "skip" (the event, step, phase, or turn is replaced with nothing) [614.1b] [Skip], "[This permanent] enters with...," "As [this permanent] enters...," or "[This permanent] enters as..." [614.1c], and "As [this permanent] is turned face up..." [614.1e]. But "instead" is the single most common marker.

question: Can a replacement effect be created (by casting a spell or activating an ability) after the event it's meant to replace has already happened, and still change that outcome?
answer:
No. A replacement effect must already exist before the event it would replace occurs; it cannot "go back in time" and change something that has already happened [614.4]. A replacement effect is a continuous "shield" that watches for a particular event that *would* happen and replaces it with a different event as it happens [614.1, 614.1a]. Once the event has occurred, there is nothing left to replace.

Practically, this means you must cast the spell or activate the ability in response to whatever would cause the event, so that it resolves before the event happens. The classic example: you may activate a regeneration ability in response to a spell that would destroy your creature, but once that spell has resolved and the creature is destroyed, it's too late to regenerate it [614.4]. There are no other special restrictions on creating such effects, and once created they last until they're used up or their duration expires [614.3].

The same principle applies to prevention effects, which watch for damage events: you can activate a damage-prevention ability in response to a spell that would deal damage, but once that spell resolves and the damage is dealt, it's too late to prevent it [615.4, 615.1].

Two related points: if you do create a replacement effect in time but the event never actually happens, the effect simply does nothing (and generally waits, per its duration) [614.7]. And note that a replacement effect can become applicable because *another* replacement or prevention effect modified the event into something it watches for — that's not "going back in time," since both effects existed before the event [616.2].

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; it applies the same in two-player and multiplayer games. (In multiplayer games using the limited range of influence option, a replacement effect that already exists can still fail to do part of what it says if it would affect something outside its controller's range of influence [801.13a].)

question: If a permanent has an effect like "if a creature you control would deal damage to a player, it deals double that damage instead," does that replacement effect apply once, or does it keep reapplying to its own already-doubled result?
answer:
It applies only once. A replacement effect doesn't invoke itself repeatedly — it gets exactly one opportunity to affect a given event, including any modified event that replaced the original ([614.5]). So a creature that would deal 2 damage deals 4, and the doubling effect does not then see "4 damage would be dealt" and re-double it into an infinite loop.

Doubling damage means the source instead deals twice that much damage, and this is a replacement effect ([701.10g]), so the general replacement-effect machinery applies: it acts as a "shield" that watches for the damage event and replaces it ([614.1]).

If you control two separate permanents each with that doubling ability, they are two distinct replacement effects, and each gets its own single opportunity. The first doubles 2 to 4, then the second applies to that modified event and doubles 4 to 8 — the rules explicitly give 8, not 4 and not infinite ([614.5]). When two or more replacement effects want to modify the same event, the affected player (or the affected object's controller/owner) chooses the order one at a time ([616.1a], [616.1b]); with doubling the end result is the same either way, and if multiple players must choose simultaneously those choices are made in APNAP order ([101.4]).

One edge case: if the source would deal 0 damage, no damage event happens at all, so a damage-increasing replacement effect has nothing to replace and does nothing ([614.7a]).

Multiplayer note: nothing here changes between a two-player game and a larger table — the effect still applies once per damage event. The only multiplayer-relevant wrinkle in the provided rules is ordering choices among multiple players, which uses APNAP order ([101.4], [616.1a]).

question: If a source would deal 0 damage, and an effect says damage from that source would instead be increased or redirected, does that replacement effect do anything?
answer:
No. If a source would deal 0 damage, it deals no damage at all — no damage event occurs — so a replacement effect that would increase that damage or redirect it to a different object or player has no event to replace and does nothing [120.8] [614.7a].

Why: replacement effects act like "shields" that watch for a particular event and then modify it [614.1]; they aren't locked in ahead of time. If the event never happens, the effect simply doesn't do anything [614.7]. Since 0 damage means no damage-dealing event, both damage-increasing effects (e.g. "deals double that damage") and redirection effects ("that damage is dealt to another creature/player instead," see [614.9]) find nothing to apply to.

Consequences worth knowing:
- Abilities that trigger on damage being dealt won't trigger either, since the trigger event never occurred [120.8] [603.2g].
- A prevention/replacement "shield" that ends up preventing or replacing no damage isn't used up — it stays available for the next time that source would deal damage [609.7b].

This answer is the same regardless of the number of players; nothing here depends on player count (multiplayer only matters for things like choosing among multiple applicable replacement effects in APNAP order [616.1e] [101.4], which doesn't arise when there's no event at all).

question: Is regeneration a triggered ability that goes on the stack, or is it a replacement effect?
answer:
Regeneration is a replacement effect, not a triggered ability, and it never goes on the stack as "regeneration."

Regeneration means replacing a permanent's destruction with an alternate sequence of events [Regenerate]. Rule 614.8 states plainly that regeneration is a destruction-replacement effect: "Regenerate [permanent]" means "The next time [permanent] would be destroyed this turn, instead remove all damage marked on it and its controller taps it. If it's an attacking or blocking creature, remove it from combat." The word "instead" isn't printed on the card but is implicit. Rule 701.8c confirms a regeneration effect replaces a destruction event, and 704.5g notes that regeneration can replace the state-based-action destruction from lethal damage.

Two important distinctions:

- The spell or activated ability that *creates* the regeneration shield does use the stack (you cast/activate it normally). But that is not the same as regenerating — see 701.19c: effects saying a permanent "can't be regenerated" don't stop you from casting the spell or activating the ability; they just cause the shield not to be applied. Once that spell or ability resolves, it creates a replacement effect that waits for the next destruction event this turn [701.19a].
- If a static ability regenerates a permanent, there's no stack involvement at all, and it replaces destruction each time it would happen, not just once [701.19b].

Timing matters: replacement effects must already exist before the event, so you must create the shield in response to (before) the destruction. Once a destroy spell has resolved, it's too late to regenerate [614.4, 614.1].

Also note that abilities triggering on damage being dealt still trigger even if the permanent regenerates [614.8, 120.4b].

If multiple replacement effects (say a regeneration shield and a shield counter's effect) would apply to the same destruction event, the affected permanent's controller chooses the order, one at a time [616.1f, 122.1c]. With more than two players this is unchanged unless multiple players must choose simultaneously, in which case choices are made in APNAP order [101.4].

If it’s an attacking or blocking creature, remove it from combat.” Abilities that trigger from damage being dealt still trigger even if the permanent regenerates. See rule 701.19.

question: Is an effect that tells a player to "skip" a step, phase, or turn a replacement effect, or some other kind of effect?
answer:
It's a replacement effect. Rules 614.1b and 614.10 state plainly that effects using the word "skip" are replacement effects: "Skip [something]" means "Instead of doing [something], do nothing," so the event, step, phase, or turn is replaced with nothing. To skip a step, phase, or turn is to proceed past it as though it didn't exist [500.11].

A few consequences that follow from its being a replacement effect:

- Like all replacement effects, it isn't locked in ahead of time; it watches for the event and replaces it as it would happen [614.1].
- Once a step, phase, or turn has actually started, it can no longer be skipped; the skip effect waits for the next occurrence [614.10].
- Anything scheduled for a skipped step, phase, or turn simply doesn't happen, and anything waiting for the "next" occurrence waits for the first one that isn't skipped. Two skip effects make a player skip the next two occurrences [614.10a].
- If a skip effect also instructs a player to take another action, that action is the first thing that happens in the next step, phase, or turn that actually occurs [614.10b].

Contrast this with effects saying something "can't happen": those are not replacement effects, though they follow similar rules [614.17].

Multiplayer note: the classification is the same regardless of player count. In the Two-Headed Giant variant, an effect causing a player to skip a step, phase, or turn causes that player's whole team to do so [805.8].

Effects that use the word “skip” are replacement effects. These replacement effects use the word “skip” to indicate what events, steps, phases, or turns will be replaced with nothing.

question: Are self-replacement effects (where part of a resolving spell's own effect replaces the rest of that same effect) continuous effects that exist independently on the battlefield, the same way most replacement effects do?
answer:
No. Self-replacement effects are not continuous effects and do not exist independently the way ordinary replacement effects do. Rule 614.15 states that some replacement effects are not continuous effects; rather, they are an effect of a resolving spell or ability that replaces part or all of that same spell or ability's own effect(s), and these are called self-replacement effects.

By contrast, most replacement effects are continuous effects (rule 614.1, 609.6) that exist as ongoing "shields" around objects or players, generated either by a static ability of a permanent (rule 604.2, which lasts as long as the permanent is on the battlefield with that ability) or by the resolution of a spell or ability (rules 611.2, 611.2a). A self-replacement effect has no such independent existence or duration \u2014 it lives and dies with the resolution of the spell or ability that contains it, modifying only that spell or ability's own effect.

Two practical notes:
- The text creating a self-replacement effect is usually part of the very ability whose effect is being replaced, though it can be a separate ability, particularly when preceded by an ability word (rule 614.15).
- Ordering matters: when multiple replacement effects would apply to the same event, self-replacement effects are applied first, before other replacement effects (rule 614.15).

Nothing about this differs between a two-player game and a multiplayer game; the classification is about the effect itself, not about player count.

question: When one permanent becomes a copy of another, does it also copy the counters, marked damage, and other continuous effects that happened to be affecting the original at that moment?
answer:
No. A copy takes only the original's copiable values — the values derived from its printed text (name, mana cost, color indicator, card types, subtypes, supertypes, rules text, power, toughness, loyalty), as modified by other copy effects, by face-down status, and by "as . . . enters"/"as . . . is turned face up" abilities that set power and toughness. Counters, marked damage's source effects, status (tapped/untapped, flipped, face up/down), stickers, and other non-copy continuous effects such as type-changing, text-changing, and pump effects are NOT copied [707.2] [707.2a].

The classic example in the rules: after Chimeric Staff has activated its ability to become a 5/5 Construct artifact creature, a Clone entering as a copy of Chimeric Staff is just an artifact — not a 5/5 creature — because that type-changing effect isn't a copiable value. Clone does get Chimeric Staff's activated ability, since that comes from printed rules text, and can activate it itself [707.2].

Why: copiable values are locked in at layer 1 (sublayer 1a), where only copy effects and merge effects apply; every other continuous effect (control-changing, text-changing, type-changing, color-changing, ability-adding, and power/toughness changes) is applied in later layers, on top of the already-determined copiable values [613.1] [613.2a] [613.2c]. Counters likewise apply in later layers, not to copiable values [707.2a].

Two things people often confuse with copying:
- Enters-the-battlefield replacement and triggered abilities in the copied text do apply. A Clone copying Skyshroud Behemoth enters tapped with two fade counters, because Skyshroud Behemoth's own printed abilities say so — those counters come from the copy's own abilities, not from being copied off the original [707.5].
- Exceptions built into a copy effect can add characteristics (e.g., "except it's legendary and snow"), and whether a conditional exception applies is checked against what the copy's characteristics would be [707.9c] [707.9f]. Also, a permanent that was cast as a prototyped spell is copied with its alternative power, toughness, and mana cost [718.3d], and merged permanents use the topmost component's characteristics as a copiable effect [730.2a].

Marked damage specifically: marked damage is not a characteristic and is not part of copiable values, so it isn't copied [707.2]. Damage already marked on the permanent that becomes a copy stays marked on it (nothing in the copy process removes it); it simply doesn't gain the original's damage. If the copying is instead a new object entering the battlefield as a copy, that new object has no damage marked on it.

This answer doesn't depend on player count — it works identically in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: If a token enters the battlefield as a copy of a permanent that has an enters-the-battlefield triggered ability, does that trigger actually fire for the token?
answer:
Yes. A token that enters the battlefield as a copy of a permanent has that permanent's copiable text, including any enters-the-battlefield triggered ability, and that ability triggers for the token.

Why: an object that enters the battlefield "as a copy" or "that's a copy" of another object becomes a copy as it enters — it doesn't enter first and then become a copy. Any enters-the-battlefield triggered abilities of the copy therefore get a chance to trigger, and any replacement effects in the copied text ("enters with...", "as [this] enters...", "enters tapped") also take effect. The rules give the Wall of Omens example: a Clone entering as a copy of Wall of Omens has Wall of Omens's "When this creature enters, draw a card" ability, so the Clone's controller draws a card [707.5]. Each time an event puts permanents onto the battlefield, all permanents (including the newcomer itself) are checked for matching enters-the-battlefield triggers [603.6a].

Two related points:
- Choices aren't copied. If the copied permanent has an "as this enters, choose..." ability, the token's controller makes a fresh choice (e.g., a token copy of Voice of All picks its own color) [707.6], [614.12], [614.1c].
- The trigger fires because the token entered the battlefield, not because it was "created." A token that results from a copy of a permanent *spell* resolving is not "created" for effects that care about creating tokens, but it still enters the battlefield and so still gets its enters-the-battlefield triggers [111.13], [608.3f], [608.3a].

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table, except that ordering of simultaneous replacement-effect choices among multiple players is made in APNAP order [616.1].

question: If permanent B has already become a copy of permanent A, and permanent A's copiable characteristics change afterward, does permanent B automatically update to match?
answer:
No. Once permanent B has copied permanent A, later changes to permanent A's copiable values do not change permanent B. Rule 707.2b states plainly: "Once an object has been copied, changing the copiable values of the original object won't cause the copy to change." Permanent B's copiable values were locked in at the moment the copy effect began applying — they are the values derived from the printed text of permanent A as modified by other copy effects, face-down status, and "as ... enters"/"as ... is turned face up" abilities that set power and toughness (707.2, 707.2c). Also note that things like counters, status (tapped, flipped, face up/down, phased), and non-copy effects (such as a Giant Growth pump or a type-changing effect) on permanent A were never copied to permanent B in the first place (707.2, 707.2c).

Two related points:
- If permanent A itself later becomes a copy of something else, that's a copy effect changing permanent A's copiable values — permanent B still keeps what it already copied (707.2b, 707.4).
- The one-way exception is going forward: if a *new* copy is made of permanent A after its copiable values changed, that new copy uses the updated copiable values (707.3, 707.9a).
- Permanent B would only change if some separate effect tells it to copy again (for example, a Vesuvan Doppelganger–style upkeep ability, 707.3), or if a static ability that generates a continuous copy effect is involved; in that case the copiable values it grants are fixed at the time that effect first starts to apply (707.2c).

This is independent of player count — it works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

question: If an effect creates a copy of a spell that's on the stack, is that copy considered to have been "cast," the way the original spell was?
answer:
No. A copy of a spell that an effect puts onto the stack was not cast. Rule [707.10] states plainly that to copy a spell means to put a copy of it onto the stack, and "a copy of a spell isn't cast." The copy is still a spell in every other sense — it's a spell even though no physical card is associated with it ([707.10], [112.1a]) — so it can resolve or be countered, and its owner and controller are the player under whose control it was put on the stack ([707.10], [112.2a]).

Practical consequences: because the copy was never cast, no steps of rule 601 were performed for it — nothing was paid, no targets or modes were chosen fresh (they're copied along with the original's decisions, including X and additional/alternative costs), and abilities that trigger "whenever a player casts a spell" do not trigger for the copy ([707.10], [601.2i]). If the copy is a copy of a permanent spell, it becomes a token as it resolves and enters the battlefield, and that token isn't "created" for effects that care about creating tokens ([111.13], [608.3f]).

The important exception: some effects instruct a player to *cast* a copy of an object rather than merely copy a spell. In that case the copy really is cast — it's created in the same zone the object is in and then cast while another spell or ability is resolving, following steps 601.2a–h, after which it becomes cast and "cast a spell" triggers do apply ([707.12], [707.12a], [112.1b]). So read the effect's wording: "copy target spell" = not cast; "you may cast a copy" = cast.

Also note that a copy inherits certain casting-mode designations: a copy of an Omen spell is an Omen ([720.3c]), a copy of a bestowed Aura spell is bestowed ([702.103c]), and a copy of a prepare spell is a prepare spell ([722.3d]) — rules referring to a spell "cast as" those things apply to the copy even though the copy wasn't itself cast.

None of this depends on player count; the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

question: If a permanent spell (one that's still on the stack) is itself a copy of another permanent spell, what does it turn into as it resolves and moves to the battlefield?
answer:
It becomes a token permanent on the battlefield. As the copy of the permanent spell resolves, it stops being a copy of a spell and is put onto the battlefield as a token that has the characteristics of the spell that became it [111.13] [608.3f] [707.10f].

Key points:
- "Copy of a spell" means a duplicate put onto the stack that isn't cast; it copies the original's copiable characteristics and the choices made for it (modes, targets, value of X, etc.) [707.10]. A copy of a spell is itself a spell even though no physical card represents it [707.10f].
- Because there's no card to put onto the battlefield, the resolution step that would normally put a permanent onto the battlefield instead puts a token there [608.3f]. The normal resolution steps still apply (e.g., an Aura copy enters attached to what it was targeting) [608.3c], and a copy with no targets simply enters under its controller's control [608.3a].
- Importantly, that token is NOT "created" for purposes of replacement effects or triggered abilities that care about creating tokens (so token-doubling effects and "whenever you create a token" triggers don't apply) [111.13] [608.3f].
- If the copied permanent spell was a double-faced spell, the resulting token is a double-faced token, entering with the same face up as the spell it copied [707.10g].
- If the copy never resolves and ends up in a zone other than the stack (countered, for example), it simply ceases to exist as a state-based action [704.5e].

This works the same regardless of the number of players; the token enters under the control of the player who controlled the copy on the stack [707.10f].

question: If an object has a pair of linked abilities (where one ability refers only to things the other one did), and that object is copied, do the two abilities stay linked to each other on the copy?
answer:
Yes. When a pair of linked abilities is copied, those abilities remain linked to one another on the object that copied them [707.7]. 

"Linked abilities" means two abilities on the same object where one causes actions to be taken or objects/players to be affected, and the other refers only to those actions or objects — not to anything done by any other ability [607.1], [Linked Abilities].

On the copy, the relationship carries over exactly: one ability refers only to actions taken or objects affected by the other, and they can't be linked to any other ability the copy currently has or ever had — even if the copy has another similarly worded ability from a different source [707.7]. This works because copying acquires the object's abilities from its copiable rules text [707.2a].

Two related points:
- The same principle applies when an object *gains* a pair of linked abilities as part of the same effect (rather than by copying): they're linked on that object too, and can't link to anything else [607.5], [614.14]. The Quicksilver Elemental example in [607.5] illustrates this — only cards exiled with the Sisters of Stone Death ability could be returned by its linked ability, not cards exiled with the Arc-Slogger ability.
- One exception involving copies: if a replacement effect that generates a copy effect is linked to a triggered ability written in the same paragraph, and another copy effect is applied to that object afterward, the linked triggered ability doesn't trigger [707.9g], [603.11].

Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: What makes a game a "multiplayer game" under the rules -- is it about how many players began the game, or how many are still in it right now?
answer:
It's about how many players the game began with. A multiplayer game is defined as a game that begins with more than two players [800.1], [100.1b], [Multiplayer Game]. The current number of players still in the game doesn't change that classification.

That matters because multiplayer games can keep going after one or more players have left [800.4]. If a five-player game is down to two players, it is still a multiplayer game and still uses the multiplayer rules (including whatever optional rules that table adopted) — it does not become a "two-player game." Conversely, a game that began with exactly two players is never a multiplayer game even if some effect could somehow add players.

When a player loses or the game is a draw for them, they leave the game [104.5], and the multiplayer rules govern the consequences [800.4]. Players who have left the game generally aren't counted for effects that count opponents — for example, undaunted ignores players who have left [702.125b]. And winning still works off who's left: a player wins when all of their opponents have left the game [104.2a], with team variants handled separately [104.2c], [104.3g].

question: In a multiplayer game played between teams, who counts as a given player's opponents?
answer:
In a multiplayer game between teams, a player's opponents are all players who are not on that player's team; the other players on their own team are their teammates [102.3]. So opponent status is decided by team membership, not by seating or by who you can attack.

A few clarifications:

- In a two-player game the rule is simpler: your opponent is just the other player [102.2].
- "Your team" used on a card is shorthand for "you and/or your teammates," and in a game that isn't a multiplayer team game, "your team" just means "you" [102.4].
- Being an opponent isn't the same as being attackable. Under the shared team turns option, the whole nonactive team is the defending team and each of its players is a defending player [805.10a], while in the Alternating Teams variant you can only attack opponents seated next to you (and only their planeswalkers/battles) [811.4] \u2014 those players are still your opponents, you just can't attack them.
- Some effects count opponents; for example, Undaunted doesn't count players who have left the game [702.125b].

question: If a spell or ability uses the phrase "your team," and the game in question isn't a multiplayer team game, who does "your team" actually refer to?
answer:
"Your team" just means you.

Rule 102.4 states that a spell or ability may use "your team" as shorthand for "you and/or your teammates," and that in a game that isn't a multiplayer game between teams, "your team" means the same thing as "you." So in a normal two-player duel — or in a free-for-all multiplayer game that isn't played between teams — the phrase affects only you, because you have no teammates.

Key terms: "you"/"your" on an object refers to that object's controller (or would-be controller if a player is casting/activating it, or its owner if it has no controller) [109.5]. A "teammate" only exists in a multiplayer game between teams, where your teammates are the other players on your team and your opponents are everyone not on your team [102.3]. Team formats include Team vs. Team [808.1], Emperor [809.1], and Two-Headed Giant.

So the difference between two players and more than two: in a two-player game "your team" = you. In a multiplayer game that is *not* between teams (e.g., a free-for-all), it still just means you, since no teammates exist. Only in a multiplayer game between teams does it expand to you plus your teammates [102.4, 102.3].

question: What is each team's starting life total in a Two-Headed Giant game?
answer:
Each team starts at 30 life in a Two-Headed Giant game [810.4], [103.4a], [119.1a]. This is a shared life total: rather than each of the two players on a team having an individual life total, the team as a whole has one pool of 30 life [Shared Life Total], [Two-Headed Giant Variant]. Damage, life loss, and life gain still happen to each player individually, but the result is applied to the team's shared total  or example, Flame Rift dealing 4 damage to each player costs a team 8 total [810.9]. If a team's shared life total is 0 or less, that team loses the game [704.6a].

Standard Two-Headed Giant is two teams of two players each [810.1]. If you play the enlarged variants (Three-Headed Giant, Four-Headed Giant, etc.) with equally sized teams of more than two players, each team's starting life total increases by 15 for every player beyond the second 	eam, and the poison counters needed to lose increases by five [810.11]. So a three-player team starts at 45, a four-player team at 60.

question: What is each player's starting life total in a Commander game?
answer:
In a Commander game, each player's starting life total is 40 [903.7] [119.1c] [103.4c]. This is a variant-specific change from the normal starting total of 20 used in most games [103.4].

Commander is a variant in which each deck is led by a legendary creature designated as that deck's commander, and it uses all the normal rules of Magic with certain additions [903.1]. Once the starting player has been determined, each player sets their life total to 40 and draws a hand of seven cards [903.7].

This 40 applies whether you're playing two-player Commander or a multiplayer table \u2014 the rules give no separate number based on player count [119.1c]. Note that the related Brawl option is different: 25 life in a two-player Brawl game and 30 in a multiplayer Brawl game [903.12f].

question: When a player leaves a multiplayer game (for example, by losing), what happens to the objects that player owns?
answer:
Everything that player owns leaves the game immediately, and the leftover objects they merely controlled get exiled. In order, per rule 800.4a: (1) all objects owned by that player (see rule 109.1 — cards, copies, tokens, spells, abilities on the stack, permanents, emblems) leave the game, and any effects giving that player control of objects or players end; (2) then any objects the departing player controlled on the stack that aren't represented by cards (e.g. their triggered/activated abilities, copies of spells) cease to exist; (3) then any objects still controlled by that player — ones owned by someone else, such as a creature stolen with Bribery — are exiled. This is not a state-based action; it happens the instant the player leaves, without using the stack (405.6h). If that player had priority, priority passes to the next player in turn order still in the game.

Details and exceptions:
• Objects owned by the departing player in the ante zone do not leave the game (800.4n; ante is an optional variant, 407.1).
• Phased-out permanents owned by the departing player also leave the game, and this does not trigger zone-change abilities (702.26k). A phased-out permanent that phased out under the control of a player who left phases in during the next untap step after that player's next turn would have begun (702.26n).
• A phased-in permanent leaving the game because its owner left the game does count as "leaves the battlefield," so leaves-the-battlefield abilities trigger (603.6c, 603.10, Leaves the Battlefield).
• Nothing new can arrive under the departed player: objects don't change control to them, tokens for them aren't created, objects that would enter the battlefield or stack under their control stay put, and they can't control a player (800.4b). Objects they would own aren't created in any zone, and triggered abilities they'd control aren't put on the stack (800.4d).
• If a control-changing effect later ends and the default controller has left the game, the object is exiled at that moment (800.4c).
• Costs that a departed player would pay or choose to pay simply aren't paid (800.4f). Durations lasting until that player's next turn last until that turn would have begun (800.4m). If they left during their own turn, the turn finishes with no active player (800.4j).
• Planechase: face-up plane/phenomenon cards owned by the departing player leave the game and the planar controller turns up the next card; abilities from phenomena are an exception and stay on the stack under the new planar controller (901.10, 901.10b). Grand Melee has its own handling (901.14b).

This all applies specifically to multiplayer games (three or more players); in a two-player game a player leaving simply ends the game, so these rules never come up (800.4).

gold_text.800.4a: Unlike two-player games, multiplayer games can continue after one or more players have left the game. When a player leaves the game, all objects (see rule 109) owned by that player leave the game and any effects which give that player control of any objects or players end. Then, if that player controlled any objects on the stack not represented by cards, those objects cease to exist. Then, if there are any objects still controlled by that player, those objects are exiled. This is not a state-based action. It happens as soon as the player leaves the game. If the player who left the game had priority at the time they left, priority passes to the next player in turn order who’s still in the game. Alex casts Mind Control, an Aura that reads, “You control enchanted creature,” on Bianca’s Assault Griffin. If Alex leaves the game, so does Mind Control, and Assault Griffin reverts to Bianca’s control. If, instead, Bianca leaves the game, so does Assault Griffin, and Mind Control is put into Alex’s graveyard. Alex casts Act of Treason, which reads, in part, “Gain control of target creature until end of turn,” targeting Bianca’s Runeclaw Bears. question: If an effect would change control of an object to a player who has already left a multiplayer game, does that control change actually happen?
answer:
No. If an object would change to the control of a player who has left the game, it doesn't — the control change simply fails to happen, and the object stays under the control it already had [800.4b]. This is part of the same rule that says no token is created for a departed player, and that objects that would enter the battlefield or the stack under a departed player's control stay in their current zone [800.4b].

Related points: when a player leaves, all objects they own leave the game with them, effects giving them control of objects or players end, and any objects still controlled by them are exiled — immediately, not as a state-based action [800.4a] [405.6h]. And if a control effect on an object later ends, no other effect controls it, and its default controller has left the game, the object is exiled at that moment [800.4c].

This question is inherently multiplayer: a two-player game ends when a player leaves, so rule 800.4b only ever matters at tables of three or more [800.4b].

question: If a triggered ability would be controlled by a player who has already left a multiplayer game, does it get put on the stack?
answer:
No — it isn't put onto the stack at all. Rule [800.4d] states that in a multiplayer game, if a triggered ability that would be controlled by a player who has left the game would be put onto the stack, it isn't put on the stack. The trigger condition can still be met, but the ability simply never goes on the stack and never resolves, so nothing it would have done happens.

The example in [800.4d] illustrates this: Bianca uses Astral Slide's ability to exile Alex's Hypnotic Specter, then Bianca leaves the game. At the beginning of the next end step, the delayed triggered ability that would return Hypnotic Specter to the battlefield triggers, but because it would be controlled by Bianca, who has left the game, it isn't put onto the stack — Hypnotic Specter never returns.

Related points:
- Any abilities that were already on the stack and controlled by the departing player cease to exist as they leave, per [800.4a] (objects on the stack not represented by cards controlled by that player cease to exist), and this happens immediately without using the stack, per [405.6h].
- Similarly, objects that would be created or put onto the battlefield/stack under that player's control aren't created or don't move ([800.4b], [800.4d]).
- This rule is specific to multiplayer play; [800.4] notes that, unlike two-player games, multiplayer games continue after players leave. In a two-player game the departure of a player ends the game, so the situation doesn't arise.
- One exception worth noting: in the Planechase variant, abilities from phenomena owned by a player who left the game remain on the stack under the new planar controller ([901.10b]).

question: In a multiplayer game, does the very first mulligan a player takes count toward how many cards they'll have to put on the bottom of their library, the way it would in a two-player game?
answer:
No. In a multiplayer game, a player's first mulligan is "free" — it doesn't count toward the number of cards that player must put on the bottom of their library, nor toward the number of mulligans they may take [800.6] [103.5c]. So after one mulligan in multiplayer you draw a fresh hand of seven (your starting hand size) and put zero cards on the bottom; after two mulligans you put one on the bottom, after three you put two, and so on. Subsequent mulligans count as normal.

A mulligan means rejecting a prospective opening hand: you shuffle your hand into your library, draw a new hand equal to your starting hand size, then put a number of those cards equal to the number of mulligans you've taken on the bottom of your library in any order [Mulligan] [103.5].

In a regular two-player game, by contrast, the first mulligan does count — you'd draw seven and put one on the bottom [103.5]. The same free-first-mulligan allowance also applies in any Brawl game, even a two-player one [903.12g] [103.5c]. Under the shared team turns (e.g. Two-Headed Giant) option, the declaration order changes — each player on the starting team declares, then each other team in turn order, teammates may consult, and a player may still mulligan after a teammate has kept — but the multiplayer free first mulligan still applies [805.3a] [103.5d].

gold_text.103.5c: Each player draws a number of cards equal to their starting hand size, which is normally seven. (Some effects can modify a player’s starting hand size.) A player who is dissatisfied with their initial hand may take a mulligan. First, the starting player declares whether they will take a mulligan. Then each other player in turn order does the same. Once each player has made a declaration, all players who decided to take mulligans do so at the same time. To take a mulligan, a player shuffles the cards in their hand back into their library, draws a new hand of cards equal to their starting hand size, then puts a number of those cards equal to the number of times that player has taken a mulligan on the bottom of their library in any order. Once a player chooses not to take a mulligan, the remaining cards become that player’s opening hand, and that player may not take any further mulligans. This process is then repeated until no player takes a mulligan. A player can take mulligans until their opening hand would be zero cards, after which they may not take further mulligans. In a multiplayer game and in any Brawl game, the first mulligan a player takes doesn’t count toward the number of cards that player will put on the bottom of their library or the number of mulligans that player may take. Subsequent mulligans are counted toward these numbers as normal.

question: Does the multiplayer "free first mulligan" rule apply in a two-player Commander game?
answer:
No. The "first mulligan is free" rule is a multiplayer rule (and a Brawl rule); a two-player Commander game is not a multiplayer game, so every mulligan counts normally there.

Details:

- Rule 800.6 grants the free first mulligan only "in a multiplayer game": the first mulligan doesn't count toward the number of cards put on the bottom of the library or toward the mulligan limit. Rule 103.5c states the same, extending it to "any Brawl game."
- Rule 903.2 explicitly says a Commander game may be a two-player game or a multiplayer game. Commander itself doesn't grant a free mulligan; the free mulligan comes from the game being multiplayer, not from being Commander.
- So in a two-player Commander game you use the normal process of rule 103.5: shuffle your hand back, draw a new hand equal to your starting hand size (normally seven), then put a number of cards equal to the number of mulligans you've taken on the bottom of your library. Your first mulligan already costs one card.
- In a Commander game with three or more players (the default Free-for-All setup per 903.2 and 806.1), rule 800.6 does apply and the first mulligan is free.
- One exception worth flagging: rule 903.12g and 103.5c give the free first mulligan in *any* Brawl game, including a two-player Brawl game. Brawl is a Commander-family variant, so if you're playing two-player Brawl specifically, you do get the free first mulligan.

question: Under the limited range of influence option, can a player's creature attack an opponent who is outside that player's range of influence?
answer:
No. Under the limited range of influence option, a creature can attack only opponents that are within its controller's range of influence (plus planeswalkers controlled by those opponents and battles protected by those opponents) [801.3]. A player's "range of influence" is the maximum distance, measured in player seats, that the player can affect; players within that many seats are in range, as are objects those players control, and this explicitly covers attacking [801.2, 801.2a]. So with a range of influence of 1, you can only attack the players seated directly next to you; with a range of 2, the two players on each side.

If no opponent is within a player's range of influence at all, creatures that player controls simply can't attack [801.3]. Likewise, if an effect lets you reselect what a creature is attacking, the newly chosen player, planeswalker, or battle must also be within the attacking creature's controller's range of influence (and for a battle, its protector must be too) [508.7e].

This is inherently a multiplayer topic: limited range of influence is an option applied to multiplayer games, always used in the Emperor variant and often in games of five or more players [801.1]. It doesn't come up in a two-player game (both players are always within range of each other). Note also that separate optional rules, such as attack left/attack right [803.1a, 803.1b] or the Emperor default of attacking only immediate neighbors [809.3c], can restrict legal attacks even further; Grand Melee defaults to range of influence 1 [807.2a], while Free-for-All usually doesn't use the option at all [806.2a].

question: In a Two-Headed Giant game (which uses the shared team turns option), does each player on the active team draw their own card during the team's shared draw step, or is there just one draw for the whole team?
answer:
Each player on the team draws their own card — there is no single "team draw." Rule 805.4b states that although each team takes turns rather than each player, each player on a team draws a card during that team's draw step. Two-Headed Giant uses the shared team turns option (810.2, 805.1), so this applies.

Order of the draws: cards are always drawn one at a time, and under the shared team turns option each player on the active team performs their own draws in whatever order that team likes, then each player on each nonactive team does the same in turn order (121.2d, 805.6a). This modifies the normal APNAP order of rule 101.4 / 121.2c.

Two related points:
- Resources aren't shared apart from life total and poison counters, so each player draws into their own hand from their own library; teammates may look at each other's hands but can't manipulate each other's cards (810.5). Similarly, each player on the team may play a land during the team's turn (805.4c).
- The team that plays first skips the draw step of its first turn entirely, so neither player on that team draws then (103.8b, 800.7, 810.6).

This question is inherently multiplayer (two teams of two, rule 810.1); in a normal two-player game the single active player simply draws one card, and the team-ordering rules of 805.6a don't come up.

Once all choices have been made, the actions happen simultaneously. question: If a player leaves a multiplayer game while controlling a permanent that has a leaves-the-battlefield triggered ability, does that ability trigger, and does it go on the stack?
answer:
Short answer: yes, a phased-in permanent leaving the game because its owner left counts as a leaves-the-battlefield event and triggers such abilities — but any resulting triggered ability that would be controlled by the player who left the game is not put onto the stack, so it does nothing.

Details:

1. Departing player's own permanents. When a player leaves a multiplayer game, all objects they own leave the game immediately (this isn't a state-based action) [800.4a]. Leaves-the-battlefield abilities trigger "when a phased-in permanent leaves the game because its owner leaves the game" [603.6c]. So the trigger event does occur.

2. Whether it reaches the stack. If the triggered ability would be controlled by the player who has left the game, it isn't put onto the stack at all [800.4d]. So a permanent owned and controlled by the departing player that says "When this creature leaves the battlefield, ..." triggers but the ability never goes on the stack and never resolves. If instead the ability belongs to a permanent controlled by a player still in the game (for example, another player's "Whenever another creature leaves the battlefield..." permanent), that ability does go on the stack and resolves normally — subject to range-of-influence restrictions in variants that use them: the trigger event must happen entirely within the range of influence of the ability's source's controller [801.7a].

3. Exception — phased-out permanents. "Phasing" is the mechanic that treats a permanent as though it doesn't exist while it's phased out. Phased-out permanents owned by a player who leaves the game also leave the game, and that specifically does not cause zone-change abilities to trigger [702.26k].

4. Permanents the departing player controlled but didn't own. Those don't leave the game with them; they either revert to their owner's control or, if no effect gives control to a player still in the game, they're exiled [800.4a], [800.4c]. Exile from the battlefield is an ordinary leaves-the-battlefield zone change, and abilities controlled by players still in the game trigger and go on the stack normally.

All of this is multiplayer-specific — a two-player game simply ends when a player leaves, so these rules never come up there [800.4].

gold_text.603.6c: Trigger events that involve objects changing zones are called “zone-change triggers.” Many abilities with zone-change triggers attempt to do something to that object after it changes zones. During resolution, these abilities look for the object in the zone that it moved to. If the object is unable to be found in the zone it went to, the part of the ability attempting to do something to the object will fail to do anything. The ability could be unable to find the object because the object never entered the specified zone, because it left the zone before the ability resolved, or because it is in a zone that is hidden from a player, such as a library or an opponent’s hand. (This rule applies even if the object leaves the zone and returns again before the ability resolves.) The most common zone-change triggers are enters-the-battlefield triggers and leaves-the-battlefield triggers. Leaves-the-battlefield abilities trigger when a permanent moves from the battlefield to another zone, or when a phased-in permanent leaves the game because its owner leaves the game. These are written as, but aren’t limited to, “When [this object] leaves the battlefield, . . .” or “Whenever [something] is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, . . . .” (See also rule 603.10.) An ability that attempts to do something to the card that left the battlefield checks for it only in the first zone that it went to. An ability that triggers when a card is put into a certain zone “from anywhere” is never treated as a leaves-the-battlefield ability, even if an object is put into that zone from the battlefield.

The rules use exactly that split: the ability triggers, and it isn't put on the stack.

question: If a game-restarting effect ends a multiplayer game and starts a new one, and one of the original players had already left the game (lost) before the restart happened, is that departed player included in the new game?
answer:
No. A player who had already left the game before the restart is not part of the new game. Rule 104.6 says that when the game restarts, "All players still in the game when it restarts then immediately begin a new game," and rules 727.1/727.1a likewise specify that "All players in that game when it ended then start a new game" following rule 103's starting procedures. A player who lost and left earlier was no longer in the game at the moment it ended, so they are not among the players who begin the new game.

Some supporting detail:

- Multiplayer games explicitly continue after one or more players have left (rule 800.4b, 800.4k), so the game that gets restarted is the game consisting only of the remaining players. Rule 800.4k even confirms that a departed player never begins a turn again.
- The new game's starting player is not decided by the normal rule-103 method; it is the player who controlled the spell or ability that restarted the game (rule 727.1a), and turn order proceeds from there among the players who are in the new game (rule 103.1).
- No one wins, loses, or draws the game that was restarted (rule 727.1a) \u2014 but that doesn't undo the earlier loss of the player who had already left; it only means the restarted game itself produces no result for the players who were still in it.
- Two players vs. more than two: this scenario only arises in a multiplayer game, since a two-player game would have already ended when one player left. For any number of remaining players, the rule is the same \u2014 everyone still in the game at the restart plays the new game.
- Range of influence: if the table is using the limited range of influence option, the restart is exempt from it, so every player still in the game joins the new game regardless of range (rules 727.7 and 801.17). Again, that phrase is "all players in the game," which does not resurrect a departed player.

One gap to flag: rule 727.2 says all Magic cards involved in the restarted game are involved in the new game and that ownership doesn't change, and rule 727.5 notes effects can exempt certain cards. The rules provided here don't spell out what happens to the cards owned by a player who had already left, since that player isn't in the new game to own a library \u2014 I can't resolve that detail from the given context without guessing.

All players in that game when it ended then start a new game following the procedures set forth in rule 103, “Starting the Game,” with the following exception:
