answer_gold: No. The rule for restarting the game specifies that all players in the game when it ended start the new game -- a player who already left before the game ended is not among "the players in that game when it ended," so they don't come back for the restarted game.

question: Does activating a mana ability use up a player's priority the way casting a spell would, or can the same player still act again immediately afterward?
answer:
Activating a mana ability does not cost you priority — if you had priority before activating it, you still have priority immediately after it resolves, and you can act again right away.

Why: a mana ability is an activated or triggered ability that produces mana and follows special rules [113.4], [605.1]. It doesn't go on the stack, so it can't be targeted, countered, or responded to; it resolves immediately upon activation [605.3b]. Because nothing goes on the stack, no player gets a chance to respond, and rule [405.6c] states explicitly that if a player had priority before a mana ability was activated, that player gets priority after it resolves. Contrast casting a spell: the spell goes on the stack and, after casting, the caster retains priority only under the normal priority rules and the spell can be responded to before it resolves.

Two related points:
- You don't even need priority to activate a mana ability. You may do so whenever you have priority, whenever you're casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment, or whenever a rule or effect asks for a mana payment — even mid-cast or mid-resolution [605.3a], [117.1d], [608.2g]. For example, if declaring attackers requires a mana cost, the active player gets a chance to activate mana abilities then [508.1i]. Note that while a spell or ability is resolving, no player actually has priority, even though mana abilities may be activated [117.2e].
- A mana ability already begun can't be activated again until it has resolved [605.3c], and activating mana abilities is never mandatory [118.3c]. Any unspent mana sits in your mana pool and must be announced if you pass priority [106.4b], [117.3d].

This works identically in two-player and multiplayer games; the only multiplayer wrinkle is that when you do eventually pass, priority goes to the next player in turn order [117.3d].

Since a mana ability also never uses the stack and resolves immediately, its activator ends up right back with priority afterward, free to pass or do something else, rather than the turn simply moving on to the next player.

question: If a game begins with four players and drops down to two remaining players over the course of play, does it stop being a "multiplayer game" for rules purposes once only two players are left?
answer:
No. A "multiplayer game" is defined as a game that *begins* with more than two players ([100.1b], [800.1], [Multiplayer Game]). That status is fixed at the start of the game and doesn't change as players leave, so a game that began with four players is still a multiplayer game even when only two players remain, and section 8's multiplayer rules (including any optional rules in use, such as limited range of influence per [801.1] or attacking multiple players per [802.1]) continue to apply.

By contrast, a two-player game is one that *begins* with only two players ([100.1a]). The core rules apply to any game of two or more players either way ([100.1]).

Some practical consequences of remaining a multiplayer game:
- The game keeps going as players leave, rather than ending as soon as one player is gone ([800.4], [104.5]).
- A player still wins the moment all of that player's opponents have left the game ([104.2a]), so once the last of the four is reduced to one, that player wins — but that's the normal win rule, not a conversion to a two-player game.
- Effects that count opponents count only players still in the game (e.g., undaunted, [702.125b]).

A game that began with four players stays a multiplayer game even after it's down to its last two combatants -- for example, its starting player would still not skip their first-turn draw step under the two-player rule, since that rule only applies to games that began with exactly two players.

question: If two different players each control a separate instance of the same triggered ability, and both instances trigger off the same shared event, is it guaranteed that one specific player's version resolves before the other's, or could either one happen first depending on choices made?
answer:
It's guaranteed, not a matter of choice: the nonactive player's copy of the ability resolves first, and the active player's copy resolves last.

Why: once abilities have triggered, they aren't put on the stack immediately — they wait until a player would next receive priority, and then they're put on the stack in APNAP (Active Player, Nonactive Player) order [603.3b]. APNAP order means the active player (the player whose turn it is) acts first, then each nonactive player in turn order [101.4]. Because the active player puts their triggered ability on the stack first, it ends up lower on the stack; the nonactive player's ability goes on top of it [603.3b], [405.3]. The stack resolves top-down as players pass priority, so the last thing put on resolves first [608.1]. Hence the nonactive player's instance resolves before the active player's.

Where choice does enter: a player who controls more than one triggered ability chooses the relative order of their own abilities among themselves [603.3b], [405.3]. But that never lets a player leapfrog another player's ability — the APNAP layering is fixed. Also note the two-part process in [603.3b]: abilities whose trigger condition is not "another ability triggering" go on the stack first (in APNAP order), then the remaining ones (in APNAP order). If your two identical abilities are both in the same part, the APNAP result above holds; if one of them triggers off another ability triggering, it goes on in the second pass and would therefore be higher on the stack and resolve earlier.

Multiplayer: the same rule scales. With more than two players, the active player's ability is lowest, then each nonactive player's in turn order (usually starting with the player to the active player's left), so the ability of the last nonactive player in turn order resolves first and the active player's resolves last [101.4], [603.3b], [405.3]. In two-player games this simply means the nonactive player's instance resolves first. (In the Two-Headed Giant variant the same idea applies at the team level: the active team places all its triggered abilities in any order, then each nonactive team does [805.7].)

One assumption: I'm reading "the same shared event" as both abilities triggering simultaneously off one event, before any player has received priority since. That's the case [603.3b] governs. If instead one triggered strictly later — after a player had already received priority and the earlier ability was already on the stack — then the later ability is put on top and resolves first regardless of who controls it. Note also that the order in which the abilities actually triggered is irrelevant to stack order [508.2b], [509.2a], [510.3a], [503.1a].

It remains on the stack until it’s countered, it resolves, a rule causes it to be removed from the stack, or an effect moves it elsewhere. If multiple abilities have triggered since the last time a player received priority, the abilities are placed on the stack in a two-part process. First, each player, in APNAP order, puts each triggered ability they control with a trigger condition that isn’t another ability triggering on the stack in any order they choose. (See rule 101.4.) Second, each player, in APNAP order, puts all remaining triggered abilities they control on the stack in any order they choose. Then the game once again checks for and performs state-based actions until none are performed, then abilities that triggered during this process go on the stack. This process repeats until no new state-based actions are performed and no abilities trigger. Then the appropriate player gets priority.

Since the stack resolves top-down, a nonactive player's version of a shared trigger always resolves before the active player's version does, regardless of what either player would prefer.

question: When a spell is cast in response to another spell already on the stack, which one actually resolves first?
answer:
The spell cast in response resolves first — the later-cast spell resolves before the spell that was already on the stack. 

Why: the stack tracks the order objects were added to it, and each new object goes on top of everything already there [405.2]. Casting a spell puts it on the stack [601.2i], so a spell cast while another spell is already on the stack is "in response to" that earlier spell, and it will resolve first [117.7]. Resolution happens one object at a time: each time all players pass priority in succession, the top (last-added) object on the stack resolves [608.1] [405.5]. "Resolves" means the object's instructions are carried out and it has its effect [Resolve] [609.1].

So the earlier spell just sits on the stack and waits; it resolves only after the responding spell has finished resolving (and after players pass priority again — the active player receives priority after each spell or ability resolves [117.3b]), and only if it's still legal and on the stack.

This is the same in two-player and multiplayer games: the stack is a shared, last-in-first-out zone regardless of player count, and players pass priority in turn order. (The one exception in the provided rules is the Grand Melee variant, which uses multiple stacks, one per turn marker; there a spell must be assigned to a specific stack, and it resolves first with respect to other objects on that same stack [807.5b].)

Text itself is never an effect.
cited_text.Resolve: Resolve. When the spell or ability on top of the stack “resolves,” its instructions are followed and it has its effect. See rule 608, “Resolving Spells and Abilities.”
cited_text.807.5b: Rather than having a single stack, Grand Melee games contain multiple stacks. Each turn marker represents its own stack. If a player has priority for multiple stacks and casts a spell, activates an ability, or a triggered ability they control triggers, the player must specify which one of those stacks the spell or ability is put on. If an object on one of those stacks caused the triggered ability to trigger, the player must put it on that stack. If a resolving spell or ability on one of those stacks causes a player to cast a spell or create a copy of a spell, the new spell must be put on the same stack. If a spell or ability targets an object on one of those stacks, it must be put on the same stack as its target; it can’t target objects on multiple stacks.

answer_gold: The newer one -- the spell cast "in response to" an earlier spell or ability goes on top of the stack and resolves first, before the original spell or ability it responded to gets a chance to resolve. The stack always resolves its top (most recently added) object first once all players pass in succession.

question: If an object checks whether a spell or ability "targets only" a single object or player, does it matter how many separate instances of the word "target" that spell used to point at the same object, or does it only care that a single distinct object/player was chosen overall?
answer:
It only cares that a single distinct object or player was chosen — the number of separate instances of the word "target" doesn't matter. A check for a "[spell or ability] that targets only [something]" counts the number of different objects or players that were chosen as targets when the spell or ability was put on the stack (as modified by effects that changed those targets), not the number of targeting instances and not how many of those targets are currently legal. Rule 115.9c says explicitly that if that number is one — "even if the spell or ability targets that object or player multiple times" — the condition can still be met.

So a spell reading "Destroy target artifact and target land" that chose the same artifact land for both instances (permitted by rules 115.3 and 601.2c, since the word "target" appears in multiple places) still targets only that one permanent.

Once the "only one distinct target" test is passed, the object then checks the current state of that target as described in rule 115.9b: if the targeted object is still in the zone it's expected to be in (or the targeted player is still in the game), its current information is used even if it's no longer a legal target; if it has left that zone (or the player left the game), the target is ignored and last known information is not used.

Contrast this with the different wording "[spell or ability] with [a number of] targets" (rule 115.9a), which does count each instance separately — there, the same object chosen twice counts as two targets.

This analysis is the same regardless of the number of players at the table; nothing in these rules depends on player count.

gold_text.115.9c: Some objects check what another spell or ability is targeting. Depending on the wording, these may check the current state of the targets, the state of the targets at the time they were selected, or both. An object that looks for a “[spell or ability] that targets only [something]” checks the number of different objects or players that were chosen as targets of that spell or ability when it was put on the stack (as modified by effects that changed those targets), not the number of those objects or players that are currently legal targets. If that number is one (even if the spell or ability targets that object or player multiple times), the current state of that spell or ability’s target is checked as described in rule 115.9b.

cited_text.115.9c: Some objects check what another spell or ability is targeting. Depending on the wording, these may check the current state of the targets, the state of the targets at the time they were selected, or both. An object that looks for a “[spell or ability] that targets only [something]” checks the number of different objects or players that were chosen as targets of that spell or ability when it was put on the stack (as modified by effects that changed those targets), not the number of those objects or players that are currently legal targets. If that number is one (even if the spell or ability targets that object or player multiple times), the current state of that spell or ability’s target is checked as described in rule 115.9b.
cited_text.115.9b: Some objects check what another spell or ability is targeting. Depending on the wording, these may check the current state of the targets, the state of the targets at the time they were selected, or both. An object that looks for a “[spell or ability] that targets [something]” checks the current state of that spell or ability’s targets. If an object it targets is still in the zone it’s expected to be in or a player it targets is still in the game, that target’s current information is used, even if it’s not currently legal for that spell or ability. If an object it targets is no longer in the zone it’s expected to be in or a player it targets is no longer in the game, that target is ignored; its last known information is not used.
cited_text.115.9a: Some objects check what another spell or ability is targeting. Depending on the wording, these may check the current state of the targets, the state of the targets at the time they were selected, or both. An object that looks for a “[spell or ability] with [a number of] targets” checks the number of times any object or player was chosen as the target of that spell or ability when it was put on the stack, not the number of its targets that are currently legal. If the same object or player became a target more than once, each of those instances is counted separately.
cited_text.115.3: The same target can’t be chosen multiple times for any one instance of the word “target” on a spell or ability. If the spell or ability uses the word “target” in multiple places, the same object or player can be chosen once for each instance of the word “target” (as long as it fits the targeting criteria). This rule applies both when choosing targets for a spell or ability and when changing targets or choosing new targets for a spell or ability (see rule 115.7).
cited_text.601.2c: To cast a spell is to take it from where it is (usually the hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Casting a spell includes proposal of the spell (rules 601.2a–d) and determination and payment of costs (rules 601.2f–h). To cast a spell, a player follows the steps listed below, in order. A player must be legally allowed to cast the spell to begin this process (see rule 601.3). If a player is unable to comply with the requirements of a step listed below while performing that step, the casting of the spell is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). The player announces their choice of an appropriate object or player for each target the spell requires. A spell may require some targets only if an alternative or additional cost (such as a kicker cost) or a particular mode was chosen for it; otherwise, the spell is cast as though it did not require those targets. Similarly, a spell may require alternative targets only if an alternative or additional cost was chosen for it. If the spell has a variable number of targets, the player announces how many targets they will choose before they announce those targets. In some cases, the number of targets will be defined by the spell’s text. Once the number of targets the spell has is determined, that number doesn’t change, even if the information used to determine the number of targets does. The same target can’t be chosen multiple times for any one instance of the word “target” on the spell. However, if the spell uses the word “target” in multiple places, the same object or player can be chosen once for each instance of the word “target” (as long as it fits the targeting criteria). If any effects say that an object or player must be chosen as a target, the player chooses targets so that they obey the maximum possible number of such effects without violating any rules or effects that say that an object or player can’t be chosen as a target. The chosen objects and/or players each become a target of that spell. (Any abilities that trigger when those objects and/or players become the target of a spell trigger at this point; they’ll wait to be put on the stack until the spell has finished being cast.) If a spell says “Tap two target creatures,” then the same creature can’t be chosen twice; the spell requires two different legal targets. A spell that says “Destroy target artifact and target land,” however, can target the same artifact land twice because it uses the word “target” in multiple places.

answer_gold: It only cares about the number of distinct objects or players chosen as targets, not how many times the word "target" was used to point at them. If a spell targets the same single object or player multiple times (once for each instance of the word "target" in its text), it still counts as "targeting only" that one object or player.

question: If a permanent's activated ability has a restriction like "activate only once each turn," and that permanent is then copied by a fresh copy effect after the ability has already been used up for the turn, does the new copy inherit the used-up restriction, or does it start the turn fresh?
answer:
A separate permanent that becomes a copy starts fresh — it can activate the ability that turn, even though the original permanent has already used up its "activate only once each turn" for the turn.

Why: the restriction is tracked per object, not per ability text. Rule 602.5b says a use restriction like "Activate only once each turn" continues to apply to that object (even if its controller changes) — i.e., it's the individual permanent that is "used up." Rule 602.5c adds that a restriction attached to an activated ability acquired from another object applies only to that acquired ability and not to other, identically worded abilities. So the copy's version of the ability is its own instance, with its own once-per-turn allowance.

Copying also doesn't carry over the fact that the ability was used. Rule 707.2a says a copy acquires only the copiable values — those derived from printed text (name, mana cost, color indicator, types, rules text, power/toughness/loyalty), as modified by other copy effects, face-down status, and "as . . . enters" abilities that set P/T; other effects, status, counters, and stickers are not copied. "I already activated this ability this turn" is game history about a particular object, not a copiable characteristic, so the new copy has no such history.

Timing assumption: I'm reading the question as one permanent activating its ability, and then a *different* object (a clone-style permanent, whether it entered as a copy per rule 707.5 or was turned into a copy by a later copy effect) becoming a copy of it. Under that reading, the new copy may activate once that turn. If instead you mean the very same permanent that already activated is merely given new copiable text (it's still the same object), then rule 602.5b keeps the restriction on that object and it cannot activate again this turn.

Related note: rule 700.10 says a permanent "that was activated this turn" means that permanent was the source of an ability activated this turn — again object-by-object, so the fresh copy wasn't "activated this turn" just because the thing it copies was.

Player count doesn't change any of this; the provided rules (602.5b in particular) are written per object and per controller, so the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

gold_text.602.5b: A player can’t begin to activate an ability that’s prohibited from being activated. If an activated ability has a restriction on its use (for example, “Activate only once each turn”), the restriction continues to apply to that object even if its controller changes.
gold_text.707.2: When copying an object, the copy acquires the copiable values of the original object’s characteristics and, for an object on the stack, choices made when casting or activating it (mode, targets, the value of X, whether it was kicked, how it will affect multiple targets, and so on). The copiable values are the values derived from the text printed on the object (that text being name, mana cost, color indicator, card type, subtype, supertype, rules text, power, toughness, and/or loyalty), as modified by other copy effects, by its face-down status, and by “as . . . enters” and “as . . . is turned face up” abilities that set power and toughness (and may also set additional characteristics). Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied. Chimeric Staff is an artifact that reads, “{X}: This artifact becomes an X/X Construct artifact creature until end of turn.” Clone is a creature that reads, “You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield.” After a Staff has become a 5/5 Construct artifact creature, a Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of it. The Clone is an artifact, not a 5/5 Construct artifact creature. (The copy has the Staff’s ability, however, and will become a creature if that ability is activated.) Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of a face-down Grinning Demon (a creature with morph {2}{B}{B}). The Clone is a colorless 2/2 creature with no name, no types, no abilities, and no mana cost. It will still be face up. Its controller can’t pay {2}{B}{B} to turn it face up.
gold_text.400.7: An object that moves from one zone to another becomes a new object with no memory of, or relation to, its previous existence. This rule has the following exceptions.
gold_text.403.4: Whenever a permanent enters the battlefield, it becomes a new object and has no relationship to any previous permanent represented by the same card, except for the cases listed in rule 400.7. (This is also true for any objects entering any zone.)

cited_text.602.5b: A player can’t begin to activate an ability that’s prohibited from being activated. If an activated ability has a restriction on its use (for example, “Activate only once each turn”), the restriction continues to apply to that object even if its controller changes.
cited_text.602.5c: A player can’t begin to activate an ability that’s prohibited from being activated. If an object acquires an activated ability with a restriction on its use from another object, that restriction applies only to that ability as acquired from that object. It doesn’t apply to other, identically worded abilities.
cited_text.707.2a: When copying an object, the copy acquires the copiable values of the original object’s characteristics and, for an object on the stack, choices made when casting or activating it (mode, targets, the value of X, whether it was kicked, how it will affect multiple targets, and so on). The copiable values are the values derived from the text printed on the object (that text being name, mana cost, color indicator, card type, subtype, supertype, rules text, power, toughness, and/or loyalty), as modified by other copy effects, by its face-down status, and by “as . . . enters” and “as . . . is turned face up” abilities that set power and toughness (and may also set additional characteristics). Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied. A copy acquires the color of the object it’s copying because that value is derived from its mana cost or color indicator. A copy acquires the abilities of the object it’s copying because those values are derived from its rules text. A copy doesn’t wind up with two values of each ability (that is, it doesn’t copy the object’s abilities and its rules text, then have that rules text define a new set of abilities).
cited_text.707.5: An object that enters the battlefield “as a copy” or “that’s a copy” of another object becomes a copy as it enters the battlefield. It doesn’t enter the battlefield, and then become a copy of that permanent. If the text that’s being copied includes any abilities that replace the enters-the-battlefield event (such as “enters with” or “as [this] enters” abilities), those abilities will take effect. Also, any enters-the-battlefield triggered abilities of the copy will have a chance to trigger. Skyshroud Behemoth reads, “Fading 2 (This creature enters with two fade counters on it. At the beginning of your upkeep, remove a fade counter from it. If you can’t, sacrifice it.)” and “This creature enters tapped.” A Clone that enters the battlefield as a copy of a Skyshroud Behemoth will also enter the battlefield tapped with two fade counters on it. Wall of Omens reads, “When this creature enters, draw a card.” A Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of Wall of Omens. The Clone has the Wall’s enters-the-battlefield triggered ability, so the Clone’s controller draws a card.
cited_text.700.10: Some cards refer to a permanent “that was activated this turn.” This means that the permanent was the source of an ability that was activated this turn, regardless of whether that permanent still has that activated ability or the player who activated it is still in the game.

answer_gold: The new copy starts fresh and can use the ability again this turn. A "once each turn" restriction is tracked per object, and it does keep following an object even if that object's controller changes -- but a copy created by a copy effect is a brand-new object with no memory of its previous existence, so it isn't the same object that already used the ability and hasn't used its own copy of that restricted ability yet this turn.
